questions.stem: An engineer is configuring the network infrastructure for an EKS cluster. They need to ensure that private subnets can access the internet for software updates but do not expose internal resources directly. Based on the script provided, which component is created in the public subnets to facilitate this outbound connectivity for the private subnets?

options.text: Internet Gateway
NAT Gateway
Elastic IP Address
Route Table

questions.explanation: The script creates NAT gateways (`Cluster_1_NGW_1` and `Cluster_1_NGW_2`) in the public subnets. Later, routes are added to the private route tables pointing to these NAT gateways, allowing private subnets to initiate outbound connections.

optionRationale.a: The Internet Gateway is attached to the VPC and used by the public route table, but the NAT Gateway is the specific component placed in public subnets to serve private subnets.
optionRationale.c: Elastic IP Addresses are allocated and associated with the NAT Gateways, but the NAT Gateway itself is the network component providing the service.
optionRationale.d: Route tables are logical collections of rules, not the network appliance providing the translation service.

questions.stem: You are validating a Hubble installation and run `kubectl get configmap -n kube-system cilium-config -oyaml | grep hubble-disable-tls`. The output shows `hubble-disable-tls: "false"`. What does this tell you before you proceed with the remaining validation steps?

options.text: TLS has been configured correctly for Hubble, because the option that would disable it is set to false.
TLS is currently disabled for Hubble and must be switched on before any further validation can take place.
The value is a placeholder written by the Hubble CLI pod, which has not yet been created in the cluster.
Hubble Relay is running, but the Hubble server certificate has expired and must be renewed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to verify the configuration before beginning, and states that you should see the `hubble-disable-tls` configuration option set to `false`. A value of `false` therefore means TLS is not being disabled, that is, it has been configured correctly, and you can continue with the validation procedure.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the meaning of the flag: `false` means TLS is not disabled, so it is not a signal that TLS must be switched on.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt presents the check as the first step, performed before the Hubble CLI pod is created, and attaches no placeholder meaning to the value.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing here about certificate expiry; expiry is not what this configuration option reports.

questions.stem: An engineer has an existing `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` that pods on the cluster are already using, and wants to modify that resource in place. Which modification does the excerpt say is possible?

options.text: Extending the pool by adding a new IPv6 CIDR alongside the existing ones.
Replacing an in-use IPv4 CIDR with a different range in a single apply.
Removing one of several CIDRs from the pool while keeping the others.
Shrinking an in-use CIDR to a smaller range so that fewer addresses are handed out.

questions.explanation: Updates to an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` are subject to limitations: the pool can be extended by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but CIDRs already in use cannot be deleted or updated. Replacing, removing or shrinking an in-use CIDR therefore falls on the forbidden side of that line. The excerpt adds that if you have no other choice than updating in-use CIDRs, the node-group migration procedure should be used as a reference instead.

optionRationale.b: Replacing an in-use CIDR is an update to a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt says is not possible; the worked example only gets there by splitting the cluster into two node groups and migrating workloads.
optionRationale.c: Removing a CIDR is a deletion of a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt explicitly rules out.
optionRationale.d: Shrinking an in-use CIDR is still an update to a CIDR already in use, so it is not among the permitted changes.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.

questions.stem: You run two clusters joined by Cluster Mesh. A global Service named rebel-base already exists, and in cluster 1 you run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=local --overwrite`. You then curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1 while healthy backends exist in both clusters. What do you observe?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only, because the local backends are preferred while they remain healthy.
The replies come from pods in both clusters, because a global Service always balances across every cluster.
The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only, because the annotation pushes traffic away from the local cluster.
No replies arrive until the annotation is removed, because the local preference blocks remote endpoints permanently.

questions.explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to local makes the Global Service prefer healthy backends in the local cluster. Remote endpoints are used only as a fallback, so a client in cluster 1 keeps being served by cluster 1 pods for as long as those backends are available and healthy.

optionRationale.b: This is the behaviour without any affinity preference; the local value deliberately overrides it while local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: That is the effect of the remote value, not the local value.
optionRationale.d: Remote endpoints are not blocked permanently; they are used if and only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity

questions.stem: Continuing with the same global Service, you now run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite` in cluster 1 and curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1. What is the result?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only.
The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only.
The replies come from pods in both clusters as usual.
The request fails, because a cluster cannot prefer endpoints it does not host.

questions.explanation: Switching the annotation to remote inverts the preference: the endpoints of the other cluster become the preferred destination, so a client in cluster 1 is served by cluster 2 pods.

optionRationale.b: That is what the local value produces, not the remote value.
optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour with no affinity preference, or when the client sits in the cluster that is not the preferred one.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the request succeeding and being answered by cluster 2 pods.

questions.stem: A global Service carries no `service.cilium.io/affinity` annotation at all. What preference does Cilium apply?

options.text: None — there is no preference, which is the default behaviour when the annotation does not exist.
Local — endpoints in the local cluster are preferred whenever they are available.
Remote — endpoints in remote clusters are preferred whenever they are available.
Global — the service is balanced strictly across all clusters with no local endpoints considered.

questions.explanation: The annotation accepts none, local and remote. The value none is the default and means no preference, and it is also the behaviour applied when the annotation is absent altogether.

optionRationale.b: Local is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.c: Remote is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.d: Global is not one of the listed values for this annotation; the global behaviour comes from the separate service.cilium.io/global annotation.

Through an `importedAnnotations` field on the ServiceImport.
Through a command-line flag on the Cilium agent DaemonSet.
Through the `service.cilium.io/global` annotation on the Service itself.

questions.explanation: When MCS-API is in use, the affinity annotation is not placed directly on the Service; it is specified through the ServiceExport's exportedAnnotations field.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the ServiceExport and its exportedAnnotations field, not a field on the ServiceImport.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes an annotation-based mechanism, not an agent command-line flag.
optionRationale.d: service.cilium.io/global is the separate annotation that marks a Service as global; it does not carry the affinity preference.

questions.stem: A global Service in cluster 1 has `service.cilium.io/affinity=remote` set. An operator runs `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity- --overwrite` in cluster 1, then curls the service from either cluster. What happens?

options.text: Replies come from pods in both clusters again, because the preference has been cleared.
Replies still come from cluster 2 only, because the preference is cached by the agent.
Replies come from cluster 1 only, because removing the annotation defaults to local.
The Service stops being global and only local endpoints remain reachable.

questions.explanation: Removing the affinity annotation returns the Service to the no-preference default, so traffic is once again spread over the backends of both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the behaviour changing immediately after the annotation is removed.
optionRationale.c: The default when the annotation does not exist is no preference, not local.
optionRationale.d: Only the affinity annotation is removed; the Service remains a global Service.

questions.stem: You expose Cilium's Envoy Daemonset with a Loadbalancer Service for a Gateway API ingress configuration. A colleague proposes setting externalTrafficPolicy: Local so that backend Pods can see the client source IP. What does the excerpt say about this proposal?

options.text: It is unnecessary for Cilium ingress config: source IP visibility to the backend Pod is retained via the X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address fields without setting externalTrafficPolicy: Local.

It is required, because in clusters that use kube-proxy, externalTrafficPolicy: Local is the only way to ensure source IP visibility, and the excerpt says this applies to Cilium ingress config as well.
It is required, because externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster always masquerades the source IP, so the backend Pod can never see it.
It is unnecessary, but only if the healthCheckNodePort is manually configured so that every node passes the health check.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly says that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure externalTrafficPolicy: Local to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod via the X-Forwarded-For and X-Envoy-External-Address fields. The statement that Local is the only way in kube-proxy clusters applies generally, but the excerpt says Cilium ingress config works differently.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does mention that in clusters that use kube-proxy, Local is the only way to ensure source IP visibility, but it then says that for Cilium ingress config things work differently and Local is not necessary.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that with Cluster the node may masquerade the source IP and that in many cases the backend pod may not see it; it does not say this always happens or that the pod can never see it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the healthCheckNodePort is automatically set by Kubernetes when externalTrafficPolicy: Local is set, and it does not make source IP visibility depend on manually configuring that port.

However, for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, **it is not
necessary** to configure ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` to keep the source IP
visible to the backend pod (via the ``X-Forwarded-For`` and ``X-Envoy-External-Address``
fields).

questions.stem: An engineer wants the Hubble metrics API to require clients to authenticate with certificates. She has already created a ConfigMap named hubble-metrics-ca in the kube-system namespace from a file called ca.crt. Which combination of Helm flags does the excerpt prescribe?

options.text: --set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true, --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true only
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=ca.crt
--set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true and --set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs the reader to add three flags to the Helm command to enable mTLS: the base TLS flag, the mTLS flag, and the flag naming the ConfigMap that holds the CA certificate. All three are required together.

optionRationale.b: Enabling mTLS alone omits both the base TLS flag and the name of the ConfigMap holding the CA certificate.
optionRationale.c: The name flag takes the name of the ConfigMap (hubble-metrics-ca), not the name of the file used to create it.
optionRationale.d: This omits the flag that actually enables mTLS authentication, so client certificates would not be required.

citations.title: Hubble Metrics TLS and Authentication

questions.stem: After TLS has been enabled on the Hubble metrics API, a monitoring engineer finds that Prometheus can no longer scrape the metrics endpoint. What does the excerpt say must be done to the Prometheus scrape configuration?

options.text: Update the scrape configuration to use HTTPS by setting a tls_config and provide the path to the CA certificate.
Leave the scrape configuration on HTTP, because TLS applies only to the Hubble observer API.
Switch the scrape target to HTTPS; no tls_config or CA certificate path is needed.
Provide a client certificate and key, but keep scraping over plain HTTP.

A client certificate and key are an additional requirement only when mTLS is in use.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says the scrape configuration must be updated to use HTTPS, so leaving it on HTTP is wrong.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt requires both HTTPS and a tls_config carrying the path to the CA certificate.
optionRationale.d: A client certificate and key are needed only in the mTLS case, and the scrape must still use HTTPS.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a shared cluster. They want the developers of one application team to be able to create Route objects in that team's own namespace, while ensuring those developers cannot modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in any other namespace. Which aspect of the Gateway API's design is intended to make this kind of arrangement possible?

options.text: The Ingress API is deconstructed into several Gateway API objects, each aligned to a role-based persona, so that each persona gains only the specific access and privileges its responsibilities require.
Gateway API resources carry annotations that record which team owns them, and the implementation uses those annotations to restrict who may edit the resource.
The Gateway API promotes features to API conformance, which automatically grants each namespace owner write access to the Gateway configuration.
The Gateway API provides a centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination and traffic splitting, and this centralisation removes the need for per-namespace permissions.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Gateway API is designed with role-based personas in mind, in contrast to the Ingress model, which assumes a single persona where developers manage and create ingress and service resources themselves. In more complex deployments, infrastructure providers, cluster operators and application developers are all involved, and by deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require. The excerpt gives exactly this example: application developers in a specific team could be assigned permissions to create Route objects in a specified namespace without also gaining permissions to modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in namespaces other than theirs.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite about annotations: native support of policies for external traffic means annotations are no longer required to support ingress traffic patterns. It never describes annotations as an ownership or access-control mechanism.
optionRationale.c: API conformance is mentioned only in connection with promoting common denominators as extensions are added, to maximise the ease of extending Ingress API resources. It is not described as granting namespace owners write access to the Gateway configuration.
optionRationale.d: The centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination, traffic splitting/weighting and header modification is a genuine feature in the excerpt, but it is not offered as the reason why per-persona permissions can be scoped; the role-based persona design is.

citations.title: Benefits of the Gateway API
citations.quote: By deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require.

questions.stem: An engineer creates an Ingress with an Exact path /api, an ImplementationSpecific path /api.*, a Prefix path /api, and a Prefix path /. A request for /api arrives. In the Envoy configuration that Cilium generates, which path's match is ordered first?

options.text: The Exact path /api
The ImplementationSpecific path /api.*
The Prefix path /api
The Prefix path /

questions.explanation: Cilium orders Envoy matches by path type: Exact first, then ImplementationSpecific (regular expression), then Prefix, with the / Prefix match always last. The Exact /api match therefore precedes the ImplementationSpecific /api.* and the Prefix /api matches.

optionRationale.b: ImplementationSpecific matches are ordered after Exact matches, so /api.* is not first even though it is a regex path.
optionRationale.c: Prefix matches are ordered after both Exact and ImplementationSpecific matches.
optionRationale.d: The / Prefix match has special handling and always goes last, not first.

citations.title: Ingress Path Types and Precedence
citations.quote:
#. Exact
#. ImplementationSpecific (that is, regular expression)
#. Prefix
#. The ``/`` Prefix match has special handling and always goes last.

questions.stem: An engineer runs Cilium 1.16 with the Gateway API enabled and switches on host network mode, because no LoadBalancer Service is available in the development cluster. One Gateway listener is configured on port 8080 and a TCPRoute is attached to that Gateway. What should the engineer expect to happen to the TCPRoute traffic?

options.text: It bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which is now a NodePort Service using a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than port 8080.
It is proxied through Envoy and served on port 8080 on all host interfaces, exactly as configured on the listener.
Host network mode is refused and the Gateway remains in LoadBalancer Service mode until the TCPRoute is removed.
It is served on port 8080, but only on the loopback interface, because host network mode binds listeners to 0.0.0.0.

questions.explanation: Host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly. That Service would normally expose the configured Gateway listener port as a LoadBalancer Service, but enabling host network mode turns it into a NodePort Service, which receives a randomly assigned port from the node port range instead of the port configured on the listener. The engineer should therefore not assume that port 8080 is the port actually serving the TCPRoute traffic.

optionRationale.b: This describes the normal Envoy-proxied path on the configured listener port, but TCPRoute and UDPRoute traffic bypasses Envoy under host network mode and the generated Service becomes a NodePort Service with a random port.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute, not that enabling it is refused; the mode is enabled and the Service type changes instead.
optionRationale.d: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6), not on the loopback interface, and the port is not the configured listener port for these route types.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling host network mode turns this Service into a ``NodePort`` Service instead, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the ``Gateway`` listener.

questions.stem: You apply a `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` that denies all traffic by default, then run `curl --fail -v http://"$HTTP_INGRESS"/details/1` against the Cilium Ingress. According to the excerpt, what happens?

options.text: The request is denied: curl reports HTTP 403 Forbidden, and the Hubble flow shows the HTTP request DROPPED with a 403 response FORWARDED.
The request succeeds with HTTP 200 OK because the default-deny policy applies only to in-cluster traffic, not to external traffic arriving through the Ingress.
The request is denied with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable because Envoy cannot reach any backend once the policy is applied.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so curl reports a connection timeout rather than an HTTP status code.

questions.explanation: With the default-deny `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` applied, the excerpt states that the request to the `/details` endpoint is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The curl output shows `HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden` with `server: envoy`, and the Hubble observe output shows the `http-request DROPPED` followed by an `http-response FORWARDED` carrying the 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the request is denied for external and in-cluster traffic, so external traffic through the Ingress is not exempt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden response, not a 503 Service Unavailable.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows an HTTP 403 response being returned, not a TCP-level connection timeout.

citations.title: Default Deny Ingress Policy
citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

questions.stem: A platform team has installed the standard release channel CRDs for Cilium Gateway API and now wants to use HTTPRoute Retry, which the excerpt identifies as an experimental feature in the HTTPRoute resource. What must the team do?

options.text: Install the corresponding CRDs; the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus experimental resources and fields.
Nothing further: the standard release channel already includes all experimental resources and fields.
Install the optional TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet CRDs, because those optional CRDs enable experimental HTTPRoute fields.
Only enable the Cilium Gateway API controller with Helm or Cilium CLI; the choice of CRD release channel has no bearing on experimental features.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. It gives HTTPRoute Retry in the HTTPRoute resource as an example of an experimental feature and states that, if you need such a feature, you must install the corresponding CRDs. The team therefore needs the corresponding CRDs, not merely the standard channel.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the excerpt: the experimental channel adds experimental resources and fields beyond the standard channel.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt lists TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet as optional CRDs for their own functionality; it does not say they enable HTTPRoute Retry.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use Helm or Cilium CLI to enable the Cilium Gateway API controller once CRDs are installed, but it separately states that experimental features require the corresponding CRDs.

citations.title: Installation
citations.quote:
Note that the **experimental** release channel includes everything in the **standard**
release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. If you need
a feature that is currently marked as *experimental* (for example, HTTPRoute Retry in the ``HTTPRoute`` resource),
you must install the corresponding CRDs.

questions.stem: A team exposes a service through Cilium Ingress. A request from outside the cluster reaches the per-node Envoy and is then sent to a backend Pod with the `productpage` identity. The team is writing Network Policy and wants the request to pass both logical policy enforcement points. Which pair of allowances must the policy provide?

options.text: Allow traffic from `world` to `ingress`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.
Allow traffic from `world` directly to `productpage`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to `world`.
Allow traffic only from `world` to `ingress`; the second enforcement point does not need a policy allowance.
Allow traffic only from `ingress` to `productpage`; external traffic is always assigned the `productpage` identity.

questions.explanation: Cilium Ingress has two logical policy enforcement points: one before traffic arrives at the `ingress` identity and one after, when it is about to exit the per-node Envoy. The policy must therefore allow traffic from `world` to `ingress` and from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the required direction and skips the `ingress` identity; the excerpt requires `world` to `ingress` and `ingress` to in-cluster identities.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says there are two logical enforcement points, so allowing only the first step is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says traffic from outside the cluster is usually assigned the `world` identity, not `productpage`; the second step alone is insufficient.

citations.title: Cilium's ingress config and CiliumNetworkPolicy
citations.quote:
This means that, when applying Network Policy to a cluster, it's important to
ensure that both steps are allowed, and that traffic is allowed from ``world`` to
``ingress``, and from ``ingress`` to identities in the cluster

questions.stem: You have deployed the `pod-worker` client and the `echo` server, confirmed that `pod-worker` receives HTTP `200` from `http://echo:3000/headers` while `http://echo:3000/headers-1` is denied, and verified that the SPIRE server is healthy. According to the excerpt, what must you add to enforce mutual authentication between `pod-worker` and `echo`?

options.text: Add `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `echo` Service definition.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the SPIRE server configuration.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that, assuming the SPIRE server is healthy, adding mutual authentication simply requires adding `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies. It does not say to modify the Service, the Pod manifest, or the SPIRE server configuration.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `echo` Service definition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to verify that the SPIRE server is healthy, but it places `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the SPIRE server configuration.

citations.title: Mutual Authentication Example
citations.quote:
adding mutual authentication simply requires 
adding ``authentication.mode: "required"`` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium Gateway API behind a trusted cloud load balancer. The load balancer injects an `X-Forwarded-For` header containing the original client IP. The team wants Cilium's Layer 7 policies, including Ingress, to be applied using that client IP rather than the address of the load balancer connection. Which configuration change matches the Cilium documentation?

options.text: Set `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` section of the values files.
Set the trusted hop count to `1` so Envoy uses the rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` value for policy decisions.
Set `useRemoteAddress` to `true` so Envoy trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header.
Do nothing, because Envoy already uses `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that when you trust the traffic source to inject an `X-Forwarded-For` header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header by setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` sections of values files. The trusted-hop count changes how Envoy derives the visible source address for `X-Forwarded-For`, and `X-Envoy-External-Address` is a header Envoy sets; neither is the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the `X-Forwarded-For` client IP.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the trusted-hop count as controlling which `X-Forwarded-For` value Envoy uses for the visible source address, not as the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt specifies setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false`, not `true`, to force Envoy to treat traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Envoy sets `X-Envoy-External-Address` to the trusted client address, but it does not say that this header is already used as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

questions.stem: A Cilium cluster has WireGuard transparent encryption enabled. Two pods that are both scheduled on the same node exchange traffic with each other, and an engineer watching the node's traffic expects to see that traffic protected by the WireGuard tunnel. What does Cilium actually do with these packets?

options.text: It leaves them unencrypted, because traffic destined to the same node it was sent from is deliberately not encrypted.
It encrypts them, because WireGuard is enabled cluster-wide for every Cilium-managed endpoint.
It encrypts them only when the two pods belong to different namespaces.
It drops them unless a CiliumNetworkPolicy explicitly allows pod-to-pod traffic on that node.

questions.explanation: WireGuard encryption in Cilium covers traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes. When the source and the destination are the same node, the packets are not encrypted, and the excerpt states that this behaviour is intended: the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway, so encryption would provide no benefit.

optionRationale.b: Enabling WireGuard does not encrypt every packet; the same-node case is explicitly excluded from encryption.
optionRationale.c: Namespace membership plays no part in the decision — the criterion given is whether the traffic is destined to the node it was sent from.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about dropping same-node traffic; it says such packets are simply not encrypted.

citations.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
citations.quote:
Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which
they were sent. This behavior is intended.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a Cilium cluster whose nodes are spread across several routing domains, and the routers in the underlying network have no knowledge of the cluster's PodCIDRs. According to the excerpt, what does the encapsulation model require of that underlying network?

options.text: The underlying network must be configured with the PodCIDRs so that its routers can forward pod traffic.
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant, provided the cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.
All cluster nodes must sit within a single link-layer domain for encapsulated traffic to flow.
The PodCIDR size must be chosen to fit within the addressing limitations of the underlying network.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists simplicity as an advantage of the model: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs, and cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains. The only requirement stated is reachability between nodes using IP/UDP, which makes the underlying topology irrelevant. Options a, c and d each contradict a specific statement in the excerpt.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains, so a single link-layer domain is not required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the addressing space does not depend on any underlying networking limitations, so the PodCIDR need not be fitted to them.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant as long as
  cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.stem: In Cilium's encapsulation model, what purpose does the excerpt give for carrying the source security identity as metadata in the network packet?

options.text: It encrypts the packet payload between the cluster nodes.
It is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.
It lets the remote node learn the PodCIDR of the sending node.
It removes the need for cluster nodes to reach each other using IP/UDP.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that encapsulation protocols allow metadata to be carried along with the network packet, and that Cilium uses this to transfer metadata such as the source security identity. It then states that this identity transfer is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node. The other options describe functions the excerpt does not attribute to the identity transfer.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt describes metadata transfer for the source security identity, not encryption of the payload.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link the identity transfer to PodCIDR discovery; it concerns the source security identity.
optionRationale.d: Node reachability over IP/UDP is described separately as a property of the model, not as something the identity transfer removes.

citations.title: Advantages of the model
citations.quote:
The identity transfer is an optimization
  designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.

questions.stem: An operator holds CAP_SYS_ADMIN in their own current user namespace and uses pod exec to enter a running Cilium agent container. Under what condition does this amount to privileged access?

options.text: Only if CAP_SYS_ADMIN is also held in the Cilium user namespace, which is the initial namespace.
Only if the operator also holds CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the Cilium container.
Always, because the Linux kernel permits joining other namespaces by default.
Only if the Cilium agent's volumes were mounted with unsafe options.

questions.explanation: The kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, so entering the Cilium container requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the current user namespace and the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace). When both namespaces carry that capability, the access is already privileged. Holding CAP_NET_ADMIN, kernel defaults or volume mount options play no part in this test.

optionRationale.b: CAP_NET_ADMIN is not the capability named in the excerpt; the test is CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so mount options are not the deciding factor.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: To enter the Cilium container, the ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN`` capability is required in both the current user namespace and in the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace).

questions.stem: A platform team discovers that developers can freely exec into Cilium pods in a shared cluster. Which two things does the excerpt say must be restricted to prevent privileged access to Cilium pods?

options.text: Access to the Kubernetes API and arbitrary pod exec operations.
Access to the /proc filesystem and the agent's Linux capabilities.
Volume mounts on the host and hostPath volume usage.
User namespace creation and the agent's CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability.

questions.explanation: The excerpt's closing recommendation is to restrict access to the Kubernetes API and arbitrary pod exec operations. That follows from the earlier point that unrestricted pod exec lets a remote user exec into pods and containers, defeating Linux namespace restrictions. The other options name mechanisms the excerpt never presents as the controls to apply.

optionRationale.b: The /proc filesystem is described as a reason Cilium needs kernel interfaces, not as something to restrict.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so volume mounts are not the control named.
optionRationale.d: CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the capability required to enter the container; the excerpt does not recommend removing it from the agent.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: To prevent privileged access to Cilium pods, restrict access to the Kubernetes API and arbitrary ``pod exec`` operations.

questions.stem: Why does the Cilium agent need kernel interfaces that cannot be virtualized or namespaced?

options.text: Because some kernel interfaces are part of the /proc filesystem, which includes host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.
Because Cilium mounts host volumes with unsafe options that bypass namespaces.
Because the Cilium agent runs without any Linux capabilities at all.
Because Kubernetes does not support user namespaces on cluster nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that Cilium needs kernel interfaces to configure the environment properly, and that some of these interfaces sit in the /proc filesystem, which carries host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced. The remaining options contradict the excerpt, which says Cilium needs specific Linux capabilities and performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says Cilium doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt opens by stating the Cilium agent needs some specific Linux capabilities.
optionRationale.d: User namespace support is not discussed; the limitation given is about /proc contents, not Kubernetes support.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: Some kernel interfaces are part of the ``/proc`` filesystem, which includes host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.

questions.stem: A security reviewer asks whether the Cilium agent itself performs extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount. How does the excerpt answer?

options.text: No: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes, and performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
Yes: the agent mounts /proc directly using privileged mount options.
Yes: the agent needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN specifically in order to mount host volumes.
No: the agent mounts no volumes at all in a Cilium deployment.

questions.explanation: The excerpt contrasts Cilium's behaviour with what a reviewer might fear: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes, and it doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount. Saying it mounts nothing at all is also wrong, since the excerpt refers to mounting the corresponding volumes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
optionRationale.c: CAP_SYS_ADMIN appears in the excerpt as the capability needed to enter the Cilium container, not as a mount requirement.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to mount the corresponding volumes, so it is not true that no volumes are mounted.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes. Cilium doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.

questions.stem: An auditor finds that a user who is not a cluster administrator can exec into a Cilium pod and reach beyond the container's namespace boundaries. According to the excerpt, what is the root cause of this exposure?

options.text: Pod exec operations are not restricted, so remote exec into pods and containers defeats Linux namespace restrictions.
The Linux kernel allows joining other namespaces by default, so no capability is ever needed.
The Cilium agent runs in the initial user namespace without any capabilities.
The /proc filesystem is virtualized per container, so exec bypasses it.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if pod exec operations aren't restricted, then remote exec into pods and containers defeats Linux namespace restrictions. The kernel does not permit namespace joining by default, and the agent does need specific Linux capabilities, so the other explanations invert the excerpt's facts.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, and that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is required in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the Cilium agent needs some specific Linux capabilities, and that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is required in the Cilium user namespace.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says some kernel interfaces in /proc include host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: If ``pod exec`` operations aren't restricted, then remote `exec into pods`_ and containers defeats Linux namespace restrictions.

questions.stem: An engineer is validating TLS for Hubble. They create the Hubble CLI pod and run `hubble watch peers`; the output lists peers but does not include a `TLS.ServerName` field. According to the excerpt, what does this indicate and what should the engineer do?

options.text: TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server, the following validation steps will not work, and the engineer should refer to the previous sections to enable TLS.
TLS is enabled, but the Hubble Relay client certificate is missing; the engineer should install OpenSSL in the Hubble CLI pod to inspect the handshake.
The `hubble-disable-tls` option is set to `true`; the engineer should edit the `cilium-config` ConfigMap and set it to `false`.
The peer is a control-plane node, which does not expose `TLS.ServerName`; the engineer should connect only to a worker peer.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if the `TLS.ServerName` is missing from the `hubble watch peers` output, TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server and the following steps will not work. It directs the reader to the previous sections to enable TLS. Installing OpenSSL is described later as a way to troubleshoot the connection and inspect the TLS handshake, not as the response to a missing `TLS.ServerName`.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that a missing `TLS.ServerName` means the Relay client certificate is missing; it says TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server. OpenSSL is used later to get more details about the TLS handshake.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says to verify that `hubble-disable-tls` is set to `false` before beginning, but it does not say that a missing `TLS.ServerName` specifically means this option is set to `true` or that the fix is to edit the ConfigMap.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not distinguish worker and control-plane peers in this way; it says that if `TLS.ServerName` is missing, TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server.

citations.title: Validating the Installation
citations.quote: If the ``TLS.ServerName`` is missing from your output then TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server and the following steps will not work.

questions.stem: A platform engineer runs the described fortio load test against echo-service:8080 with two concurrent connections and 20 requests. The summary reports 19 responses with code 200 and one with code 503. After increasing the number of concurrent connections to four, the output shows several 'Non ok http code' warnings with 503. What does the excerpt say the 503 response code does?

options.text: It triggers a circuit breaker.
It indicates that fortio has exhausted its client-side connection pool.
It shows that echo-service has no available endpoints.
It is a client-side artefact rather than a server response.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that 'the response code of some requests is 503' and that this 'triggers a circuit breaker'. The first run reports one 503 among 20 responses, and raising the concurrency to four produces repeated 503 warnings, consistent with the circuit breaker being triggered.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not attribute the 503 responses to a fortio connection-pool limit; it says the 503 response code triggers a circuit breaker.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not state that echo-service has no available endpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt treats the 503 as a response code observed in the output that triggers a circuit breaker, not as a client-side artefact.

citations.title: Tripping Envoy Circuit Breaker
citations.quote:
From the above output, you can see that the response code of some requests is 503, 
which triggers a circuit breaker.

questions.stem: An operator finds that a node is reaching the default limit for authenticated relations in the Auth BPF map and wants to raise that map's upper capacity limit for cilium-agent. Which option should they use?

options.text: --bpf-auth-map-max
--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio
--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max
--bpf-lb-map-max

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that for some BPF maps the upper capacity limit can be overridden using command-line options for cilium-agent, and it lists --bpf-auth-map-max as the option for setting a given capacity. The Auth map has a default limit of 512k, with the scale implication of a maximum of 512k authenticated relations per node, so this is the relevant flag for raising that limit.

optionRationale.b: This flag determines the upper capacity limits of several large BPF maps at agent startup based on a ratio of total system memory; the excerpt does not list the Auth map among the maps it affects.
optionRationale.c: This flag sets a capacity for the connection tracking global TCP map, not for the Auth map.
optionRationale.d: This flag sets a capacity for the load-balancing map, not for the Auth map.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `kubectl get gateway -A` and sees a Gateway in the `website` namespace with class `cilium` and an address, but the `PROGRAMMED` column does not show `True`. According to the excerpt, what should the engineer check?

options.text: Make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.
Check that a LoadBalancer implementation is present.
Check that the Gateway's class is `cilium`.
Install the Gateway API CRDs.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if the `Programmed true` indicator is missing, you should make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration. The other checks address different symptoms: a missing address points to a possible missing LoadBalancer implementation, a non-`cilium` class is not programmed by Cilium, and a missing Gateway API resource type points to missing CRDs.

optionRationale.b: This is the check suggested when no IP address appears for the Gateway, but the scenario says the Gateway has an address.
optionRationale.c: The scenario already states that the Gateway's class is `cilium`, and the excerpt says Cilium only programs Gateways with the class `cilium`.
optionRationale.d: This is the check suggested when the Gateway API resource type is not found, but the scenario has already found a Gateway resource.

citations.title: Checking resources
citations.quote: If the ``Programmed true`` indicator is missing, make sure that Gateway API is enabled in the Cilium configuration.

questions.stem: You are troubleshooting an Ingress. After connecting with SSH to a Kubernetes node, you send a request to localhost on the node port shown for the LoadBalancer service and receive an HTTP 503 response that includes the header `server: envoy`. According to the excerpt, what does this response indicate?

options.text: The request is being redirected to the Cilium Envoy proxy successfully.
The cloud load balancer has not forwarded traffic to the node port, so the first troubleshooting step has failed.
The Cilium Envoy proxy is not running on the node, which is the most common root cause.
The backend service is healthy and the Envoy Discovery Service has resolved its endpoints.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that a response similar to the one shown means the request is being redirected to proxy successfully, and that the response will carry the special header `server: envoy`. The 503 status does not establish that the backend is healthy.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the first step between the cloud LoadBalancer and the node port is out of Cilium scope; a `server: envoy` response from the node port does not show that this step failed.
optionRationale.c: A `server: envoy` response indicates that the request was redirected to the proxy successfully, so it does not support the conclusion that the proxy is not running.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt advises double-checking whether the backend service is up and healthy; the 503 response with `server: envoy` does not establish backend health or EDS resolution.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If you see a response similar to the above, it means that the request is being
redirected to proxy successfully. The http response will have one special header
``server: envoy`` accordingly.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a global Service named rebel-base across two clusters in Cluster Mesh. In cluster 1, the Service already has service.cilium.io/global: "true". An engineer in cluster 1 runs kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite, then runs kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should the engineer observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in cluster 2 only.
Replies from pods in cluster 1 only.
Replies from pods in both clusters as usual.
No replies, because remote affinity is only honoured when the annotation is set through a ServiceExport exportedAnnotations field.

questions.explanation: With service.cilium.io/affinity set to remote in cluster 1, the remote endpoints are preferred. The excerpt states that when cluster 1 accesses the global Service after this change, the replies come from pods in cluster 2 only. The local-only outcome belongs to the local affinity case, while the both-cluster outcome belongs to the default/no-preference case and to access from cluster 2.

optionRationale.b: This is the outcome described for affinity local, not remote: with local, cluster 1 sees replies from cluster 1 only.
optionRationale.c: This is the outcome described for the default/no-preference case and for access from cluster 2, not for remote affinity from cluster 1.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say remote affinity produces no replies; it says the replies come from cluster 2 only. The MCS-API note concerns how to specify the annotation, not a condition that blocks traffic.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: This time, the replies are coming from pods in ``cluster 2`` only.

questions.stem: Your cluster uses the multi-pool IPAM mode. A single CiliumPodIPPool named default currently lists 10.10.0.0/16, and running pods on two nodes hold addresses from that range. You want those workloads to receive addresses from 10.20.0.0/16 instead. According to the excerpt, what must you do?

options.text: Split the cluster into two node groups and migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.
Replace 10.10.0.0/16 with 10.20.0.0/16 in the pool and restart the existing pods so they pick up addresses from the new CIDR.
Delete the existing CiliumPodIPPool and recreate it with 10.20.0.0/16; existing pods will then be re-assigned addresses from the new CIDR automatically.
Add 10.20.0.0/16 as an additional CIDR and remove 10.10.0.0/16 in the same apply so that new pods use only the new range.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that changing a pool's CIDR requires re-assigning the IPs of existing workloads, and that this is achieved by splitting the cluster into two node groups so workloads can migrate from nodes using the old CIDR to nodes using the new CIDR. Simply replacing the CIDR in the pool is not enough: the excerpt notes that it is not possible to delete or update CIDRs already in use, and the operator warns about CIDRs still in use by nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says it is not possible to delete or update CIDRs already in use; replacing the CIDR in the pool does not re-assign existing workload IPs.
optionRationale.c: Deleting and recreating the pool does not by itself re-assign the IPs of existing workloads; the excerpt's procedure requires node groups and workload migration.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt permits extending a pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it explicitly says you cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use, so removing the old CIDR in the same apply is not allowed.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: which allows you to migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.

questions.stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that contains two ingress rules. The first rule matches a broad set of traffic, and the second matches a narrower set that overlaps with the first. A colleague is concerned that the narrower rule will somehow cut down what the broader rule permits. How does Cilium treat traffic that matches either of the two rules?

options.text: It is allowed, because the rules are additive: traffic matching the union of the rules is permitted.
It is allowed only if it matches the narrower rule, because the more specific rule takes precedence over the broader one.
It is allowed only where the two rules do not overlap, because intersecting rules cancel each other out.
It is allowed only if it matches both rules at once, because the rules in a policy are combined with a logical AND.

questions.explanation: Cilium policy rules follow a whitelist model: each rule allows the traffic that matches it, and rules are additive rather than subtractive. Where two rules overlap, the traffic matching the union of those rules is allowed, so adding a narrower rule alongside a broader one does not remove anything the broader rule already permitted. The colleague's concern is therefore unfounded. Note that traffic which matches none of the rules is dropped pursuant to the `policy_enforcement_modes`.

optionRationale.b: There is no precedence for a more specific rule in the whitelist model; a narrower rule simply adds its own matches to those of the broader rule rather than overriding it.
optionRationale.c: Rules do not cancel one another out on overlap; the excerpt states that traffic matching the union of intersecting rules is allowed.
optionRationale.d: Rules are not combined with a logical AND requiring a match against every rule; each rule independently allows the traffic that matches it.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote: If there is an intersection between two or more rules, then traffic matching the union of those rules will be allowed.

questions.stem: Which statement about where BGP peering problems surface, according to the guide, is correct?

All BGP peering failures are guaranteed to appear in the Cilium logs.
Low-level connectivity errors always appear in the logs, while BGP layer errors never do.
BGP peering failures are only visible in the peer router logs, never in Cilium logs.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly allows for cases where low-level errors may not be reflected in the logs, so no guarantee is given.
optionRationale.c: This reverses the guide: BGP layer errors are likely to appear, while some low-level errors may not.
optionRationale.d: The guide says you can identify the cause by referring to the logs of your peer router or Cilium, so Cilium logs are a valid source.

questions.stem: An engineer runs `cilium-dbg status --verbose` on a cluster where kube-proxy replacement is active. Which of the following does the verbose output report?

options.text: Mode: SNAT, with Socket LB Enabled and protocols TCP, UDP
Mode: DS NAT, with Socket LB Disabled and protocols TCP only
Mode: Hybrid, with Socket LB Enabled and protocols UDP only
Mode: SNAT, with Socket LB Disabled and protocols SCTP, TCP, UDP

A wildcard would also admit names the engineer did not list, and toFQDNs is an L3 egress rule, not the DNS query policy.

questions.stem: A team is configuring Layer 7 DNS policy and is deciding which DNS traffic to intercept. What does the excerpt strongly recommend?

Avoid interception entirely and rely on matchPattern alone.

optionRationale.c: The recommendation names the cluster DNS service as the preferred interception target, not external resolvers.
optionRationale.d: Interception is the mechanism by which the DNS proxy collects IPs; the excerpt recommends narrowing it, not abandoning it.

Query types only, with names handled by toFQDNs rules.
All DNS header fields, including query type and response code.

optionRationale.d: The excerpt names query type as an example of a field that is not considered, so not all header fields are used.

questions.stem: You are tracing socket load-balancing events with Hubble and want to confirm that a client's connection to a ClusterIP service is being translated to a backend pod. In the Hubble output, which event indicates the flow after the service address has been translated to the selected endpoint?

options.text: A `pre-xlate-fwd` event showing the client talking to the service address
A `post-xlate-fwd` event showing the client talking to the backend pod address
A `pre-xlate-rev` event showing the backend pod talking to the client
A `post-xlate-rev` event showing the service address talking to the client

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Hubble prints datapath events before and after socket LB translation between service and selected service endpoint, and the sample output shows the `post-xlate-fwd` event carrying the backend pod (`default/nginx:80`) rather than the service address. That is the forward direction after translation.

optionRationale.a: `pre-xlate-fwd` is the event before translation, still showing the service address, not the translated endpoint.
optionRationale.c: `pre-xlate-rev` is a reverse-direction event before translation, not the forward translated flow.
optionRationale.d: `post-xlate-rev` is a reverse-direction event after translation, not the forward translated flow.

optionRationale.c: Listing services is unrelated to the socket LB tracing failure described.
optionRationale.d: Re-deploying the client pod is not mentioned as a remedy for the tracing setup failure.

questions.stem: A cluster administrator is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that includes a `toPorts` entry with both an `http` rule list and a `dns` rule list for the same port. What is the outcome?

options.text: The policy is rejected, because mixing different port level rule types in a single port is disallowed.
Both rule sets are applied, with HTTP evaluated before DNS.
The DNS rules are silently ignored and only the HTTP rules take effect.
The policy is accepted but the port is treated as having no layer 7 rules.

questions.explanation: The `L7Rules` structure is a union: exactly one of the protocol-specific fields must be set per port, and mixing different port level rule types is disallowed. Supplying both `http` and `dns` for the same port therefore makes the policy invalid.

optionRationale.b: The union design forbids combining members on one port, so they are not both applied in any order.
optionRationale.c: Silently dropping one member is not what the excerpt describes; mixing is disallowed outright.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that if none are specified no additional port level rules apply, but here two conflicting types are specified, which is a rejection case.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
The structure is implemented as a union, i.e. only one member field can be used
per port.

questions.stem: Two `toPorts` rules in a policy have identical `PortProtocol` values and select an overlapping set of endpoints. One carries HTTP layer 7 rules and the other carries DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The layer 7 rules are combined, with HTTP taking precedence over DNS.
The policy is rejected, because the layer 7 rule types differ.
Only the first rule encountered is used and the second is discarded.
Both rules are applied independently to the endpoints without interaction.

questions.explanation: When multiple `toPorts` rules with identical `PortProtocol` select an overlapping list of endpoints, layer 7 rules are combined only if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.a: Combining happens only for rules of the same type; differing types cause rejection, not precedence.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes combining or rejecting, not first-match discarding.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selection with identical `PortProtocol` triggers the combine-or-reject rule, so they are not treated independently.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select
an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together
if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

questions.stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints, and also a similar layer 4 rule for the same endpoints that additionally carries layer 7 rules. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion?

options.text: It is enforced in addition to the plain layer 4 rule.
It has no effect.
It causes the whole policy to be rejected.
It overrides the plain layer 4 rule entirely.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, the layer 7 portions of the latter rule will have no effect.

optionRationale.a: The layer 7 portion is neutralised, not added to the plain layer 4 rule.
optionRationale.c: Rejection applies to differing layer 7 types on overlapping `toPorts` rules, not to this situation.
optionRationale.d: The layer 7 portion has no effect; it does not replace the plain layer 4 rule.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
If a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy, and a similar layer 4 rule
with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the
latter rule will have no effect.

questions.stem: An HTTP request violates a layer 7 policy rule. According to the excerpt, what does Cilium do where possible?

options.text: It drops the packet silently at the network layer.
It crafts an application protocol specific access denied message, such as an HTTP 403 access denied.
It resets the TCP connection without any application response.
It returns a DNS REFUSED response for the HTTP request.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says layer 7 policy violations do not result in packet drops; instead, where possible an application protocol specific access denied message is crafted, for example an HTTP 403 access denied for HTTP requests.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says violations do not result in packet drops.
optionRationale.c: A TCP reset is not mentioned; the described behaviour is an application-level denial message.
optionRationale.d: A DNS REFUSED response applies to DNS requests, not HTTP requests.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote:
not result in packet drops. Instead, if possible, an application
          protocol specific access denied message is crafted and returned, e.g.
          an *HTTP 403 access denied* is sent back for HTTP requests which
          violate the policy

optionRationale.c: The excerpt explicitly says it does not cover the Hubble UI, and describes Relay as offering the API consumed by the UI.
optionRationale.d: The Unix domain socket is a local consumption path for the Hubble server, not a cluster-wide aggregator.

questions.stem: An engineer applies a CiliumNetworkPolicy selecting a pod, but traffic to and from that pod is not being restricted. The pod is running with host networking. According to the excerpt, what is the reason policy enforcement is not working, and what can be done about it?

options.text: The pod uses the host's IP address directly, so Cilium does not enforce policy for it by default; set hostNetwork to false or use HostPolicies to enforce policy against it.
The pod was started before Cilium, so it must be restarted before any policy can apply to it.
The pod's ingress and egress rules were applied but silently dropped because the Cilium operator is not ready.
Host-networked pods are always managed by Cilium, so the problem must be a malformed policy selector.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists host networking as a situation producing unmanaged pods: such pods use the host's IP address directly and Cilium will not provide security policy enforcement for them by default. It states that to enforce policy against these pods you either set `hostNetwork` to false or use HostPolicies.

optionRationale.b: Restarting is the remedy given for pods started before Cilium was deployed, not for host-networked pods.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe rules being silently dropped due to operator readiness; it says ingress and egress policy rules selecting unmanaged pods will not be applied.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: host-networked pods are unmanaged by default and get no policy enforcement.

The pod is running in host networking and will use the host's IP address

questions.stem: A cluster had several workloads running for some time before Cilium was installed. Policies selecting those older pods appear to have no effect. What does the excerpt say is the cause and the recommended action?

The pods are managed but the policy rules are invalid; the policies must be rewritten using HostPolicies.
Cilium manages all pods regardless of when they started, so the cause must be that the Cilium CLI was not run.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that a pod started before Cilium was deployed is unmanaged: Cilium only manages pods deployed after Cilium itself was started, and such pods should be restarted so that Cilium can provide security policy enforcement.

optionRationale.a: Host networking is a separate cause listed in the excerpt; nothing here indicates these pods use it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not attribute this to invalid rules, and HostPolicies are mentioned only in relation to host-networked pods.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says Cilium only manages pods deployed after Cilium itself was started, so this contradicts the source.
