questions.stem: An operator is running Cilium's DSR NodePort mode and observes problems in an environment where TCP Fast Open (TFO) is enabled. According to the excerpt, what is recommended?

options.text: Switch to `snat` mode.
Disable the eBPF kube-proxy replacement and use iptables kube-proxy.
Enable BPF-based masquerading instead of iptables masquerading.
Enable the socket-LB feature so that TFO traffic is translated in the cgroup hooks.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that DSR NodePort mode does not currently operate well with TCP Fast Open enabled, and recommends switching to `snat` mode in that situation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt recommends switching to ``snat`` mode, not abandoning the eBPF kube-proxy replacement.
optionRationale.c: BPF-based masquerading is recommended over iptables when using BPF-based NodePort, but it is not the remedy given for TFO with DSR.
optionRationale.d: socket-LB is described in relation to service translation and libceph, not as a fix for TFO with DSR NodePort.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium's DSR NodePort mode currently does not operate well in environments with
      TCP Fast Open (TFO) enabled. It is recommended to switch to ``snat`` mode in this
      situation.

questions.stem: A platform team mounts NFS volumes to a `Service` cluster IP while using socket-LB, and the mounts break. They want to avoid the problem by ensuring their kernel carries the relevant fixes. Which commit does the excerpt list as required for SMB only?

options.text: `cedc019b9f26 ("smb: use kernel_connect() and kernel_bind()")`
`0bdf399342c5 ("net: Avoid address overwrite in kernel_connect")`
`86a7e0b69bd5 ("net: prevent rewrite of msg_name in sock_sendmsg()")`
`01b2885d9415 ("net: Save and restore msg_namelen in sock_sendmsg")`

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists four commits to include in the underlying kernel, and marks the `cedc019b9f26` commit with the note `(SMB only)`, distinguishing it from the other three.

optionRationale.b: This commit is listed without an SMB-only qualifier.
optionRationale.c: This commit is listed without an SMB-only qualifier.
optionRationale.d: This commit is listed without an SMB-only qualifier.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote: ``cedc019b9f26 ("smb: use kernel_connect() and kernel_bind()")`` (SMB only)

questions.stem: A pod is configured with a `hostPort` that overlaps with the configured NodePort range, on a cluster using Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement. What does the excerpt say happens?

options.text: The `hostPort` setting is ignored and a warning is emitted to the Cilium agent log.
The Pod is rejected by the Cilium agent and remains in a pending state.
The NodePort range is automatically extended so that both configurations can coexist.
The `hostPort` takes precedence and the overlapping NodePort is disabled.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the eBPF kube-proxy replacement does not allow `hostPort` configurations for Pods that overlap with the configured NodePort range; in such a case the `hostPort` setting is ignored and a warning is emitted to the Cilium agent log.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the setting being ignored with a warning, not the Pod being rejected.
optionRationale.c: No automatic extension of the NodePort range is described.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``hostPort`` setting is ignored, not that it takes precedence.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
In such case, the ``hostPort``
      setting will be ignored and a warning emitted to the Cilium agent log.

questions.stem: Which statement about transport protocol support in Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement matches the excerpt?

options.text: SCTP is not supported except in a few basic cases, and only TCP and UDP are fully supported as a transport for services at this time.
SCTP is fully supported, while UDP is supported only in a few basic cases.
TCP, UDP and SCTP are all fully supported as service transports.
Only SCTP is fully supported as a service transport, with TCP and UDP limited to basic cases.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the eBPF kube-proxy replacement does not support SCTP except in a few basic cases, and that only TCP and UDP are fully supported as a transport for services at this time.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt reverses this: SCTP is the limited protocol, and UDP is fully supported.
optionRationale.c: SCTP is explicitly excluded from full support.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says TCP and UDP are fully supported, not SCTP.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
Cilium's eBPF kube-proxy replacement does not support the SCTP transport protocol except
      in a few basic cases.

questions.stem: You have created a single VNet peering from cluster one's virtual network to cluster two's virtual network using `az network vnet peering create` with `--allow-vnet-access`. What connectivity does this give you?

options.text: Outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two only; the reverse direction needs a second peering.
Full bi-directional traffic, because a single peering is always symmetric.
No traffic at all until a route table is attached to both virtual networks.
Only traffic between the control planes, not node-to-node traffic.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the first peering command allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two, and that bi-directional traffic requires adding a peering in the other direction as well.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says virtual networks can't connect by default and that bi-directional traffic requires a peering in the other direction too, so one peering is not symmetric.
optionRationale.c: No route table is mentioned anywhere in the excerpt; the peering itself is what enables cross-VNet communication.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt makes no distinction between control-plane and node traffic; it speaks of outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
This allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two. To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

questions.stem: An engineer has run the peering command from cluster one to cluster two and now wants node-to-node traffic between the clusters to work in both directions. What must be done next according to the excerpt?

options.text: Add a peering from cluster two to cluster one, using cluster one's VNet ID as the remote VNet.
Re-run the same command with `--allow-vnet-access` removed so the peering becomes symmetric.
Delete the first peering, since two peerings on the same pair of VNets conflict.
Nothing further; node-to-node traffic is already possible after the first peering.

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows a second `az network vnet peering create` command that peers cluster two's VNet back to cluster one, looking up cluster one's VNet ID, and then states that node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never suggests removing `--allow-vnet-access`; both example commands include it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say the first peering must be deleted; it says to add a peering to the other direction as well.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says node-to-node traffic is possible only after the second, reverse peering is added.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

questions.stem: In the excerpt's first peering command, how is the remote virtual network supplied to `az network vnet peering create`?

options.text: Via `--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}"`, where `VNET_ID` was obtained with `az network vnet show --query id -o tsv`.
Via `--vnet-name`, which is set to the remote cluster's network name.
Via `--resource-group`, which points at the remote cluster's resource group.
Via `--name`, which is set to the remote peering's name.

questions.explanation: The excerpt first exports `VNET_ID` using `az network vnet show` with `--query id -o tsv`, then passes it to the peering command as `--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}"`.

optionRationale.b: `--vnet-name` is set to the local cluster's network (`${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net`), not the remote one.
optionRationale.c: `-g`/`--resource-group` is set to the local cluster's group (`${CLUSTER1}-group`).
optionRationale.d: `--name` names the peering itself (`peering-${CLUSTER1}-to-${CLUSTER2}`), not the remote VNet.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
--remote-vnet "${VNET_ID}" \
     --allow-vnet-access

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the default state of virtual network connectivity and the mechanism the excerpt uses to change it?

options.text: Virtual networks can't connect by default; cross VNet communication is enabled by creating bi-directional peering.
Virtual networks are connected by default and peering is only needed to restrict traffic.
Virtual networks connect automatically once both clusters exist in the same subscription.
Cross VNet communication requires a VPN gateway rather than peering.

questions.explanation: The excerpt opens by stating that virtual networks can't connect to each other by default and that cross VNet communication is enabled by creating bi-directional peering.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: connection is not the default, and peering enables communication rather than restricting it.
optionRationale.c: No automatic connection based on subscription is described; the excerpt requires explicit peering commands.
optionRationale.d: VPN gateways are not mentioned; the excerpt names peering as the mechanism.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
Virtual networks can't connect to each other by default. You can enable cross
VNet communication by creating bi-directional "peering".

questions.stem: After completing the peering in both directions, what does the excerpt conclude about the state of the clusters with respect to Cilium Cluster Mesh?

options.text: Node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible and all requirements for clustermesh are met.
Node-to-node traffic is possible but a further step is still required before clustermesh requirements are met.
Clustermesh is already fully enabled by the peering commands themselves.
Node-to-node traffic remains impossible until a load balancer is provisioned.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible and that all requirements for clustermesh are met, with enabling clustermesh explained elsewhere.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says all requirements for clustermesh are met, not that a further requirement remains.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says enabling clustermesh is explained in gs_clustermesh, so the peering commands do not themselves enable it.
optionRationale.d: Load balancers are not mentioned in the excerpt at all.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
Node-to-node traffic between clusters is now possible. All requirements for
clustermesh are met.

questions.stem: When creating the reverse peering from cluster two to cluster one, which resource group and VNet name does the excerpt's command target?

options.text: `-g "${CLUSTER2}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER1}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER2}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net"`.
`-g "${CLUSTER1}-group"` with `--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"`.

questions.explanation: In the second command block the peering is created in cluster two's resource group and VNet, with cluster one's VNet ID used as the remote VNet.

optionRationale.b: Those are the local values used in the first command block, which peers cluster one to cluster two.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt pairs cluster two's resource group with cluster two's VNet name, not cluster one's.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt pairs cluster one's resource group with cluster one's VNet name in the first block, not the reverse block.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
-g "${CLUSTER2}-group" \
     --name "peering-${CLUSTER2}-to-${CLUSTER1}" \
     --vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"

questions.stem: An operator notices that every pod in a Deployment is receiving its own distinct security identity rather than sharing one identity across the application. The pods carry a label whose value is a deployment timestamp. What does the excerpt recommend to address this?

options.text: Limit the set of identity-relevant labels so that labels such as timestamps are not evaluated for identity.
Convert the timestamp label into an annotation so that Cilium ignores it automatically.
Add an inclusive label pattern for the timestamp label so that it is grouped across pods.
Disable identity allocation entirely for the namespace containing the Deployment.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that operators with larger environments should limit the set of identity-relevant labels to avoid frequent creation of new security identities, and gives timestamps and hashes as examples of labels that are not useful for policy enforcement or visibility. Such labels, when included in evaluation, cause Cilium to generate a unique identity for each pod instead of a single identity for all pods of a service or application.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that annotations are ignored automatically; it lists an exclusive pattern for annotation labels, and nothing about converting labels to annotations.
optionRationale.c: An inclusive pattern restricts relevance to matching labels; it does not group a per-pod unique value into a shared identity.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about disabling identity allocation for a namespace.

citations.title: Limiting Identity-Relevant Labels
citations.quote:
We recommend that operators with larger environments limit the set of
identity-relevant labels to avoid frequent creation of new security identities.

questions.stem: An operator adds a single inclusive label pattern to the identity-relevant label configuration. Which of the following label patterns is then automatically added to the configuration?

options.text: `app\.kubernetes\.io`
`!pod-template-hash`
`!topology\.kubernetes\.io`
`!annotation.*`

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that once at least one inclusive label pattern is added, only labels matching the inclusive configuration may be considered relevant, and a set of inclusive label patterns is automatically added, including `app\.kubernetes\.io` to include all `app.kubernetes.io` labels.

optionRationale.b: ``!pod-template-hash`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.
optionRationale.c: ``!topology\.kubernetes\.io`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.
optionRationale.d: ``!annotation.*`` is an exclusive pattern from the default exceptions list, not one of the automatically added inclusive patterns.

questions.stem: After installing SPIRE with the default configuration, you inspect the cilium-spire namespace and see two spire-agent pods and one spire-server pod. How does the excerpt say these workloads are deployed?

options.text: The SPIRE server is a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents are a DaemonSet, so you should see one SPIRE agent per node.
The SPIRE server is a DaemonSet and the SPIRE agents are a StatefulSet, so you should see one SPIRE server per node.
Both the SPIRE server and the SPIRE agents are deployed as Deployments with a single replica each.
The SPIRE server is a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents are bare pods created directly, one per node.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the SPIRE server is deployed as a StatefulSet and the SPIRE agents as a DaemonSet, which is why one agent appears per node.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two workload types; the server is the StatefulSet and the agents the DaemonSet.
optionRationale.c: No Deployment appears in the excerpt; the resources listed are a DaemonSet and a StatefulSet.
optionRationale.d: The agents are managed by a DaemonSet, as shown by the daemonset.apps/spire-agent entry, not created as bare pods.

optionRationale.d: The agents are a DaemonSet regardless; the excerpt does not tie workload type to the attestation strategy.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Kata Pods on a Cilium cluster with VXLAN enabled. Users report packet drops between traditional pods and Kata Pods, which the team traces to fragmentation. Which workaround does the excerpt describe as preferred?

options.text: Lower the MTU value in the Cilium ConfigMap so that the KataPod receives a lower device MTU.
Add an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to the KataPod deployment to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod.
Disable VXLAN on the cluster so that no additional networking overhead is applied to the default route MTU.
Set the runtimeClassName of the KataPod to a value that copies the default route MTU into the inner namespace.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that there are two possible workarounds, with (b) being preferred, and (b) is to modify the KataPod deployment by adding an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to adjust the route MTU inside the inner pod. It is preferred because it aligns the KataPod configuration with all other pods and does not harm other connection types, being self-contained in the KataPod itself.

optionRationale.a: This is workaround (a), which the excerpt explicitly does not recommend because of its impact on all other communications.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt never suggests disabling VXLAN; it only mentions VXLAN as an example of overhead (+50B).
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the default route MTU is ignored during inner namespace creation, and no runtimeClassName value changes that.

citations.quote: There are currently two possible workarounds, with (b) being preferred:

questions.stem: An engineer wants to find the correct route MTU value to configure inside a KataPod. According to the excerpt, how can that value be obtained?

options.text: By reading the device MTU from the Cilium ConfigMap and using it unchanged.
By issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod or inside a traditional pod, or by computing it manually.
By issuing ip route inside the inner Container Networking Namespace of the KataPod.
By adding 50B to the outer eth0 device MTU for VXLAN overhead.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the correct route MTU value can be either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ip route on a Cilium Pod (or inside a traditional pod).

optionRationale.a: The ConfigMap MTU is the device MTU, not the route MTU, which is reduced by the overhead.
optionRationale.c: The inner namespace is precisely where the route MTU is not set correctly, so it is not the suggested source.
optionRationale.d: Overhead is subtracted from the device MTU, not added to it.

citations.title: Limitations
citations.quote:
either manually computed or retrieved by issuing ``ip route`` on a Cilium Pod
(or inside a traditional pod).

questions.stem: Why does the excerpt not recommend lowering the MTU value in the Cilium ConfigMap as a fix for KataPod fragmentation?

options.text: Because the Cilium ConfigMap MTU is ignored by the Kata runtime when creating the inner eth0.
Because it would prevent the KataPod from receiving a lower device MTU at all.
Because the lower device MTU value would be set on all Cilium-managed interfaces, affecting all other types of communications.
Because it would require adding an initContainer with NET_ADMIN to every traditional pod.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says workaround (a) is not recommended as it would have a relevant impact on all the other types of communications (for example traditional pod-to-pod and pod-to-node) due to the lower device MTU value being set on all the Cilium-managed interfaces.

optionRationale.a: The ConfigMap MTU does influence the outer device MTU; the problem is its cluster-wide effect, not that it is ignored.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt says this workaround would allow the KataPod to have a lower device MTU, so it does take effect.
optionRationale.d: The initContainer approach is workaround (b), not a consequence of workaround (a).

questions.stem: An engineer is planning a Cluster Mesh between three clusters. One cluster runs Cilium 1.18.x, a second runs 1.17.x, and a third runs 1.16.x. What does the excerpt say about this combination?

options.text: It is acceptable, because all three versions are within two minor releases of each other.
It is not acceptable, because 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x, but not 1.16.x.
It is acceptable, because only the datapath mode must match across clusters.
It is not acceptable, because all clusters must run exactly the same Cilium version.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium versions must differ by no more than one minor release, and gives the example that 1.18.x can connect to 1.17.x or 1.19.x but not 1.16.x. The third cluster at 1.16.x therefore breaks the requirement.

optionRationale.a: The permitted spread is one minor release, not two; the excerpt explicitly excludes 1.16.x for a 1.18.x cluster.
optionRationale.c: Matching datapath mode is a separate requirement; the version rule is stated independently and is still violated.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt allows a difference of one minor release, so identical versions are not required.

questions.explanation: The excerpt's first requirement is that all clusters must be configured with the same datapath mode, noting that Cilium may default to arch_overlay or native_routing depending on the cloud environment. A mismatch between the two clusters therefore fails this prerequisite.

optionRationale.a: Unique PodCIDR ranges are a separate requirement and do not remedy a datapath mode mismatch.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the datapath mode as a per-cluster configuration, not a per-node choice.
optionRationale.d: Peering or VPN tunnels address node IP connectivity, which is a different requirement from datapath mode.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt refers to specific ports documented in the firewall_requirements section rather than permitting all traffic.

questions.stem: A policy uses fromRequires to require that any source endpoint must have label env=prod to reach endpoints with label env=prod. The same policy also includes a fromEndpoints rule that allows traffic from endpoints with label role=frontend. Which source endpoints will be able to reach the env=prod endpoints?

Any endpoint with role=frontend, regardless of env label.
Any endpoint with env=prod, regardless of role label.
No endpoints, because fromRequires blocks all traffic.

questions.explanation: The fromRequires rule sets a base requirement that the source must have env=prod. The fromEndpoints rule allows traffic from role=frontend. Both conditions must be met, so only endpoints with both labels can connect. The excerpt confirms this: when combined, the endpoint becomes accessible from endpoints that have both labels env=prod and role=frontend.

optionRationale.b: The fromRequires requirement for env=prod remains in effect and is not overridden by the fromEndpoints rule.
optionRationale.c: The fromEndpoints rule only allows role=frontend, so env=prod alone is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: fromRequires does not block all traffic; it only adds a requirement that must be satisfied alongside other rules.

questions.stem: An engineer is reviewing a CiliumNetworkPolicy that uses fromRequires to limit ingress to endpoints with label app=db. optionRationale.b: The fromEndpoints rule does not override fromRequires; the requirement remains.
optionRationale.c: fromRequires applies to all traffic for the endpoint selector, not just traffic not matched by fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says pairing other rules with fromRequires results in valid policy.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium with metrics enabled but has left `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` at `false`. They want Prometheus to discover the Cilium metrics endpoints without a ServiceMonitor. What does the chart provide for this?

options.text: Annotations on the Cilium components, including `prometheus.io/scrape: true` and `prometheus.io/port: 9962`.
A ServiceMonitor resource that Prometheus discovers automatically.
A headless service named `cilium-operator` carrying the scrape annotations.
Nothing; Prometheus must be pointed at each pod IP manually.

questions.explanation: With metrics enabled and ServiceMonitor disabled, all Cilium components receive the scrape annotations, and the excerpt shows `prometheus.io/scrape: true` together with `prometheus.io/port: 9962`.

optionRationale.b: A ServiceMonitor is only used when `hubble.metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled: true`, in which case the annotations are omitted instead.
optionRationale.c: The headless service the chart creates is named `cilium-agent`, and it exists to collect Envoy metrics, not operator metrics.
optionRationale.d: The annotations exist precisely so Prometheus can be signalled whether to scrape, so manual pod-IP configuration is not required.

questions.stem: You are reproducing the Cilium CNI performance benchmark on Equinix Metal hardware and want to automate the provisioning of the machines rather than clicking through the Packet web UI. Which sequence of commands does the excerpt give for this?

options.text: `cd terraform`, then `terraform init`, then `terraform apply -var 'packet_token=API_TOKEN' -var 'packet_project_id=PROJECT_ID'`, then `terraform output ansible_inventory | tee ../packet-hosts.ini`, then `cd ../`
`cd terraform`, then `terraform plan -var 'packet_token=API_TOKEN'`, then `terraform destroy`, then `terraform output ansible_inventory > packet-hosts.ini`
`cd playbooks`, then `ansible-playbook -i packet-hosts.ini packet-disbond.yaml`, then `terraform init`, then `terraform apply`
`terraform init`, then `ansible -i packet-hosts.ini all -m shell -a 'uptime'`, then `terraform apply -var 'packet_token=API_TOKEN'`

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows the Terraform workflow in a shell session: changing into the terraform directory, initialising, applying with the `packet_token` and `packet_project_id` variables, writing the `ansible_inventory` output to `../packet-hosts.ini` with `tee`, and returning to the parent directory.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never uses `terraform plan` or `terraform destroy`, and it writes the inventory with `terraform output ansible_inventory | tee ../packet-hosts.ini`, not a plain redirect.
optionRationale.c: The `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook is run later, after provisioning, and the excerpt does not place it before `terraform init`.
optionRationale.d: The ad-hoc `uptime` command is used to verify provisioning after the Terraform apply, not before it, and the apply in this option omits the `packet_project_id` variable.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
$ cd terraform
  $ terraform init
  $ terraform apply -var 'packet_token=API_TOKEN' -var 'packet_project_id=PROJECT_ID'
  $ terraform output ansible_inventory  | tee ../packet-hosts.ini
  $ cd ../

questions.stem: After running the Terraform steps, you want to confirm that the two servers were provisioned successfully. According to the excerpt, how is this verification performed?

options.text: By running an ad-hoc `uptime` command on the servers with `ansible -i packet-hosts.ini all -m shell -a 'uptime'`
By running `terraform output ansible_inventory` a second time and comparing the two outputs
By running the `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook and checking that `bond0` still exists
By inspecting the Packet web UI for the `knb` VLAN

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that you verify successful provisioning by executing an ad-hoc `uptime` command on the servers, and shows the corresponding Ansible invocation against the generated inventory.

optionRationale.b: Re-running the output command is not described as a verification step; the excerpt uses the ad-hoc `uptime` command instead.
optionRationale.c: The `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook is a later configuration step, and it destroys the `bond0` interface rather than preserving it.
optionRationale.d: The web UI is mentioned only as an alternative to the Terraform automation for setting the network mode, not as the provisioning check.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
Verify that the servers are successfully provisioned by executing an ad-hoc ``uptime``
command on the servers.

questions.stem: Which network mode do the Packet machines need in order to evaluate both arch_overlay and native_routing, and what does that mode provide?

options.text: A "Mixed/Hybrid" network mode, in which the secondary interfaces of the machines share a flat L2 network
A bridged mode, in which the primary interfaces are bonded into `bond0` for the evaluations
A routed mode, in which each machine gets a dedicated VLAN per interface
A NAT mode, in which the secondary interfaces are hidden behind the public IP

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that to evaluate both arch_overlay and native_routing the Packet machines are configured to use a "Mixed/Hybrid" network mode, where the secondary interfaces of the machines share a flat L2 network.

optionRationale.b: `bond0` is the interface that the later `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook destroys; it is not the network mode used for the evaluations.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes a flat L2 network shared by the secondary interfaces, not a dedicated VLAN per interface.
optionRationale.d: NAT is not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
To evaluate both arch_overlay and native_routing, we configure
the Packet machines to use a `"Mixed/Hybrid"
<https://deploy.equinix.com/developers/docs/metal/layer2-networking/overview/>`_ network
mode, where the secondary interfaces of the machines share a flat L2 network.

questions.stem: What does the `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook do to the machines' network interfaces?

options.text: It destroys the `bond0` interface and configures the first physical interface with the public and private IPs (`prv_ip`) and the second with the node IP (`node_ip`)
It creates a `bond0` interface combining the first and second physical interfaces
It assigns the public IP to the second physical interface and the `node_ip` to the first
It provisions the two `c3.small.x86` servers and writes the Ansible inventory

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the playbook will destroy the `bond0` interface and configure the first physical interface with the public and private IPs (`prv_ip`) and the second with the node IP (`node_ip`) used for the evaluations.

optionRationale.b: The playbook destroys `bond0` rather than creating it.
optionRationale.c: The order is the reverse: the first physical interface gets the public and private IPs, the second gets the `node_ip`.
optionRationale.d: Provisioning the servers and writing the inventory is done by the Terraform steps, not by this playbook.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
Next, we use the ``packet-disbond.yaml`` playbook to configure the network
interfaces of the machines. This will destroy the ``bond0`` interface and
configure the first physical interface with the public and private IPs
(``prv_ip``) and the second with the node IP (``node_ip``) that will be used
for our evaluations

questions.stem: You are reproducing the benchmark on a hardware platform other than Packet. What does the excerpt say you must do?

options.text: Provide your own inventory file (`packet-hosts.ini`) and follow the subsequent steps
Run the Terraform files with a different `packet_token` to target the other platform
Skip the `packet-disbond.yaml` playbook entirely, since it is Packet-specific
Change the OS from `ubuntu_20_04` to a supported alternative before proceeding

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that for hardware platforms other than Packet, users need to provide their own inventory file (`packet-hosts.ini`) and follow the subsequent steps.

optionRationale.b: The Terraform files are presented as the automation for the Packet provisioning; the excerpt does not suggest reusing them with a different token for other platforms.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says to follow the subsequent steps, not to skip the playbook.
optionRationale.d: No alternative OS is mentioned; `ubuntu_20_04` is simply what the Terraform provisioning uses.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
For hardware platforms other than Packet, users need to provide their own
    inventory file (``packet-hosts.ini``) and follow the subsequent steps.

questions.stem: Which servers and operating system does the Terraform provisioning create, and under what VLAN?

options.text: Two servers named `knb-0` and `knb-1` of type `c3.small.x86`, provisioned with an `ubuntu_20_04` OS under a common VLAN named `knb`
Two servers named `knb-0` and `knb-1` of type `c3.large.x86`, provisioned with an `ubuntu_22_04` OS under a VLAN named `cilium`
Three servers named `knb-0`, `knb-1` and `knb-2` of type `c3.small.x86` under a VLAN named `knb`
Two servers named `master` and `node` of type `c3.small.x86` under a VLAN named `packet`

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the Terraform steps provision two servers named `knb-0` and `knb-1` of type `c3.small.x86`, configured to use a "Mixed/Hybrid" network mode under a common VLAN named `knb`, with an `ubuntu_20_04` OS.

optionRationale.b: Both the machine type and the OS version are wrong; the excerpt specifies `c3.small.x86` and `ubuntu_20_04`, and the VLAN is `knb`.
optionRationale.c: Only two servers are provisioned, not three.
optionRationale.d: `master` and `nodes` are Ansible inventory group names in `packet-hosts.ini`, not the server names, and the VLAN is `knb`.

citations.title: Packet Servers
citations.quote:
The above will provision two servers named ``knb-0`` and ``knb-1`` of type
``c3.small.x86`` and configure them to use a "Mixed/Hybrid" network mode under a
common VLAN named ``knb``.  The machines will be provisioned with an
``ubuntu_20_04`` OS.

questions.stem: An engineer enables WireGuard node-to-node encryption and expects every node in the cluster to participate. Which nodes will automatically opt out of node-to-node encryption?

options.text: Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label.
Nodes carrying the node-role.kubernetes.io/worker label.
Every node that has a CiliumNode CRD registered.
No nodes opt out; node-to-node encryption always applies cluster-wide.

questions.explanation: Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to Kubernetes control-plane nodes, identified by the node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane label, which is the default value of the node-encryption-opt-out-labels option.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the control-plane label, not a worker label, as the opt-out selector.
optionRationale.c: A CiliumNode CRD exists for nodes generally and is not the opt-out criterion.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly describes an automatic opt-out, so participation is not cluster-wide by default.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
Cilium automatically disables node-to-node encryption from and to
  Kubernetes control-plane nodes, i.e. any node with the
  ``node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane`` label will opt-out of node-to-node
  encryption.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to force node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes. Which configuration achieves this, and what is the consequence?

options.text: Set node-encryption-opt-out-labels to an empty label selector; the engineer must then always manually update a node's public key in its CiliumNode CRD when a worker node's public key changes.
Set node-encryption-opt-out-labels to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane; worker nodes then update their own public keys automatically.
Remove the control-plane label from every node; no manual key maintenance is then required.
Disable WireGuard entirely; node-to-node encryption is then applied to all nodes including the control plane.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that an empty label selector with node-encryption-opt-out-labels forces node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes, and that this is not recommended because it requires always manually updating a node's public key in its CiliumNode CRD when a worker node's public key changes.

optionRationale.b: That is the default selector, which causes control-plane nodes to opt out rather than forcing encryption.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe removing labels as a mechanism, and manual key updates would still be needed.
optionRationale.d: Disabling WireGuard would remove encryption rather than extend it to the control plane.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
You may force node-to-node encryption from and to control-plane nodes by
  using an empty label selector with that option.

questions.stem: Which ConfigMap option controls the label selector for matching control-plane nodes that shall not participate in node-to-node encryption, and what is its default?

options.text: node-encryption-opt-out-labels, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.
node-encryption-opt-out-labels, defaulting to an empty label selector.
node-to-node-encryption-labels, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.
encryption-opt-out-selector, defaulting to node-role.kubernetes.io/worker.

questions.explanation: The excerpt names the node-encryption-opt-out-labels ConfigMap option and states that it defaults to node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane.

optionRationale.b: An empty selector is the value used to force encryption on control-plane nodes, not the default.
optionRationale.c: The option name is node-encryption-opt-out-labels, not node-to-node-encryption-labels.
optionRationale.d: Neither the option name nor the worker label matches the excerpt.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
The label selector for matching the control-plane nodes which shall not
  participate in node-to-node encryption can be configured using the
  ``node-encryption-opt-out-labels`` ConfigMap option. It defaults to
  ``node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane``.

questions.stem: Even with node-to-node encryption disabled on control-plane nodes, what does the excerpt say remains encrypted there?

options.text: The Kubernetes control-plane itself is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes using mTLS, and pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on those nodes is still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard implementation.
Nothing remains encrypted on control-plane nodes once they opt out.
Only N/S load balancer traffic remains encrypted on control-plane nodes.
Only Egress Gateway replies remain encrypted on control-plane nodes.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that even if WireGuard node-to-node encryption is disabled on those nodes, the Kubernetes control-plane is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes itself using mTLS, and pod-to-pod traffic for Cilium-managed pods on control-plane nodes is still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard implementation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly lists two forms of traffic that remain encrypted.
optionRationale.c: N/S load balancer traffic is described as not encrypted in certain redirection configurations, not as the remaining protection.
optionRationale.d: Egress Gateway replies are described as not encrypted when XDP Acceleration is enabled, not as remaining protection.

citations.title: Node-to-Node Encryption (beta)
citations.quote:
Note that even if
  WireGuard node-to-node encryption is disabled on those nodes, the Kubernetes
  control-plane itself is usually still encrypted by Kubernetes itself using
  mTLS and that pod-to-pod traffic for any Cilium-manged pods on the
  control-plane nodes are also still encrypted via Cilium's WireGuard
  implementation.

questions.stem: You have deployed a node-local DNS cache as a normal pod and applied a Local Redirect Policy, but DNS queries from application pods are still being resolved by the cluster DNS service rather than the cache. Which verification step does the excerpt recommend to confirm the policy has been applied on the Cilium agent pods?

options.text: Run `cilium-dbg lrp list` inside a Cilium agent pod and check that the policy appears with its matching service.
Run `cilium-dbg service list | grep LocalRedirect` and check for a `ClusterIP` entry.
Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` and check `coredns_dns_requests_total`.
Run `kubectl --namespace kube-system get pods --selector=k8s-app=node-local-dns` and check the READY column.

questions.explanation: The troubleshooting section instructs you to check whether the local redirect policy has been applied correctly on all the cilium agent pods, using `cilium-dbg lrp list`. The output shows the LRP namespace, name, frontend type and matching service.

optionRationale.b: The service list check is a separate troubleshooting step, for confirming the local redirect service entry exists, not for confirming the policy was applied on the agents.
optionRationale.c: The metrics check is how you verify that traffic is now going to the cache after the pods are ready, not a troubleshooting step for a policy that has not taken effect.
optionRationale.d: Checking that the node-local DNS pods are running and ready is a different troubleshooting step, listed before the policy check.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: Check if the local redirect policy has been applied correctly on all the cilium agent pods.

questions.stem: After all `node-local-dns` pods report ready, you want to confirm that DNS requests from application pods are actually being redirected to the node-local cache. What does the excerpt say you should do?

options.text: Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` and check that `coredns_dns_requests_total` increments as new DNS requests are issued.
Curl the `kube-dns` service VIP on port 53 and check that responses come from the cluster DNS pods.
Run `cilium-dbg lrp list` and confirm the frontend type is `clusterIP + all svc ports`.
Restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods and watch for a new local redirect service entry.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that you can verify redirection by checking the DNS cache's metrics `coredns_dns_requests_total` via curling `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics`, and that the metric should increment as new DNS requests from application pods are redirected to the `node-local-dns` pod.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe curling the kube-dns VIP; it describes curling the node-local DNS pod IP on port 9253.
optionRationale.c: Listing the LRP shows the policy configuration, but the excerpt presents the metrics check as the way to verify that traffic now goes to the local node-cache.
optionRationale.d: Restarting the DaemonSet pods is given as a workaround for a missing local redirect service entry, not as a verification method.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: You can verify by checking the DNS cache's metrics ``coredns_dns_requests_total`` via curling

questions.stem: You are enabling the DNS node-cache in a Cilium cluster. According to the excerpt, why must a Local Redirect Policy be deployed rather than relying on the node-cache's default interception?

options.text: Because the node-cache's default interception of traffic to the cluster DNS service VIP is bypassed when Cilium handles service resolution at or before the veth interface of the application pod.
Because the node-cache cannot listen on a static IP unless an LRP rewrites its listening address.
Because Cilium blocks all traffic to the `kube-dns` service until an LRP names that service as its matching service.
Because the node-cache only serves TCP queries, so an LRP is needed to add UDP support.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the DNS node-cache listens on a static IP to intercept traffic to the cluster's DNS service VIP by default, but this will be bypassed when Cilium is handling service resolution at or before the veth interface of the application pod. Hence an LRP is deployed to steer DNS traffic to the node local dns cache.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the node-cache already listens on a static IP by default; the LRP is for steering traffic, not for changing the listening address.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt says Cilium blocks traffic to `kube-dns`; the issue is that the default interception is bypassed.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the LRP using both `dns` and `dns-tcp` port names, so the node-cache is not described as TCP-only.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote:
bypassed when Cilium is handling service resolution at or before the veth interface of the
application pod

questions.stem: You are adapting the example Local Redirect Policy for a cluster whose DNS service and port names differ from the quick deployment yaml. Which adjustments does the excerpt say are needed?

options.text: Modify the LRP to specify your cluster DNS service, and modify the port names to match your deployment if they differ.
Change the LRP's namespace to the application pod namespace and keep the `dns` and `dns-tcp` port names.
Change the node-cache's static listening IP and leave the LRP unchanged.
Replace the LRP with a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that selects the `kube-dns` pods.

questions.explanation: The excerpt notes that the example LRP uses `kube-dns` for the cluster DNS service and that you will need to modify the example LRP if your cluster DNS service is different; it also says the LRP uses the same port names `dns` and `dns-tcp` as the example quick deployment yaml and that you will need to modify those to match your deployment if they are different.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the namespace specified in the LRP is set to the same namespace as the cluster's dns service, not the application pod namespace.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not mention changing the node-cache's static listening IP; it points to modifying the LRP.
optionRationale.d: No `CiliumNetworkPolicy` replacement is mentioned; the excerpt describes deploying a Local Redirect Policy.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: you will need to modify this example LRP to specify it.

questions.stem: A colleague asks what happens to DNS queries from application pods in a Cilium cluster that has no node-local DNS cache. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: They get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the `kube-dns` service.
They are dropped until a Local Redirect Policy is created.
They are answered by the Cilium agent itself at the veth interface.
They are sent to the node-local cache's static IP and time out.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that in the absence of a node-local DNS cache, DNS queries from application pods will get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the `kube-dns` service.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes normal direction to cluster DNS pods, not dropping.
optionRationale.c: Cilium handling service resolution at or before the veth interface is described as bypassing the node-cache's interception, not as answering DNS queries itself.
optionRationale.d: Without a node-local cache there is no cache static IP to send queries to in the excerpt's description.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote:
In the absence of a node-local DNS cache, DNS queries from application pods
will get directed to cluster DNS pods backed by the ``kube-dns`` service.

questions.stem: During troubleshooting you find that the local redirect service entry is missing, which the excerpt attributes to a possible race condition between applying the policy and the node-local DNS DaemonSet pod resources. What workaround does the excerpt suggest?

options.text: Restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods, and file a GitHub issue with a sysdump if the issue persists.
Delete and recreate the Local Redirect Policy, then re-run `cilium-dbg lrp list`.
Restart the Cilium agent pods so that the policy is reapplied on every node.
Curl `<node-local-dns pod IP>:9253/metrics` until `coredns_dns_requests_total` increments.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that if the service entry is missing there might have been a race condition in applying the policy and the node-local DNS DaemonSet pod resources, and that as a workaround you can restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods, filing a GitHub issue with a sysdump if the issue persists.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not suggest recreating the LRP; it suggests restarting the DaemonSet pods.
optionRationale.c: Restarting the Cilium agent pods is not mentioned as the workaround for a missing service entry.
optionRationale.d: The metrics check verifies redirection once things work; it is not the workaround for a missing service entry.

citations.title: Node-local DNS cache
citations.quote: As a workaround, you can restart the node-local DNS DaemonSet pods.

questions.stem: An operator notices that the interval at which Cilium performs its background etcd health check differs between a small cluster and a much larger one. According to the excerpt, what determines this interval?

options.text: The overall cluster size: the larger the cluster, the longer the interval.
The number of etcd endpoints that are currently unreachable.
The number of consecutive quorum failures recorded so far.
The lease ID assigned to the lock used for the write test.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says the interval depends on the overall cluster size, and that the larger the cluster, the longer the interval.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not tie the interval to how many endpoints are unreachable; unreachable endpoints lead to reported failure instead.
optionRationale.c: Consecutive failures determine when Cilium is declared unhealthy, not the length of the check interval.
optionRationale.d: The lock lease ID appears in the example status output but is not stated to influence the interval.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: The interval depends on the overall cluster size. The larger the cluster, the longer the

questions.stem: A Cilium agent can reach no etcd endpoints at all. What does the excerpt say will happen?

options.text: Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status, the Kubernetes liveness and readiness probe fail, and Cilium is restarted.
Cilium waits for three consecutive intervals before reporting anything, then declares loss of quorum.
The Cilium operator rewrites the heartbeat key so that agents can resume receiving updates.
etcd elects a new leader and the agent fails over to a healthy endpoint without any restart.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if no etcd endpoints can be reached, Cilium reports failure in cilium-dbg status, which causes the Kubernetes liveness and readiness probe to fail and Cilium to be restarted.

optionRationale.b: The three-interval threshold applies to the quorum write test and the heartbeat check, not to the case where no endpoints can be reached.
optionRationale.c: The operator constantly writes to the heartbeat key, but the excerpt does not describe it as a remedy for total unreachability.
optionRationale.d: Leader election and failover describe etcd's own recovery when an endpoint becomes unhealthy, not the agent's behaviour when no endpoint is reachable.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: If no etcd endpoints can be reached, Cilium will report failure in ``cilium-dbg status``. This will cause the liveness and readiness probe of Kubernetes to fail and Cilium will be restarted.

questions.stem: How does the excerpt distinguish the lock-based check from the heartbeat-based check in Cilium's background etcd health monitoring?

options.text: The lock check tests a write operation requiring quorum, while the heartbeat check validates that an agent can receive key updates from etcd.
The lock check validates receipt of key updates, while the heartbeat check tests a write operation requiring quorum.
The lock check is performed by the operator, while the heartbeat check is performed only by the Kubernetes probes.
The lock check runs only when no etcd endpoints can be reached, while the heartbeat check runs continuously.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says a lock is acquired and released to test a write operation which requires quorum, and separately that agents watching the heartbeat key validates the ability for an agent to receive key updates from etcd.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the two roles: the lock tests the quorum-requiring write, and the heartbeat validates receipt of key updates.
optionRationale.c: It is the operator that writes the heartbeat key, and the probes are not described as performing the lock check.
optionRationale.d: The lock check is not conditioned on total unreachability; that situation is covered by the reported failure in cilium-dbg status.

citations.title: Recovery behavior
citations.quote: A lock is acquired and released to test a write operation which requires quorum.

questions.stem: You are using the Cilium Gateway API implementation with Cilium's MCS-API. A ServiceImport resource is missing the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service`. What is the consequence according to the excerpt?

options.text: The Cilium Gateway API implementation will not support that MCS-API implementation.
The ServiceImport will be ignored by all Gateway API implementations.
Cilium will automatically add the annotation.
The HTTPRoute will fail to be created.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium Gateway API implementation only supports MCS-API implementations using an underlying Service associated with a ServiceImport, and with the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service` on ServiceImport resources. Therefore, without that annotation, the Cilium Gateway API implementation will not support that MCS-API implementation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the ServiceImport is ignored by all implementations; it specifically discusses the Cilium Gateway API implementation's requirements.
optionRationale.c: There is no mention of Cilium automatically adding the annotation; the excerpt states the annotation must be present.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that the HTTPRoute creation fails; it only describes the support conditions for the Cilium Gateway API implementation.

citations.title: Gateway-API
citations.quote:
On the other hands, the Cilium Gateway API implementation only supports MCS-API
implementations using an underlying Service associated with a ServiceImport, and with
the annotation ``multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service`` on ServiceImport resources.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about the Cilium Gateway API implementation's support for MCS-API?

options.text: It fully supports its own MCS-API implementation.
It requires EndpointSlice synchronization to operate.
It only supports MCS-API implementations that use EndpointSlice.
It does not support MCS-API at all.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explicitly states that the Gateway API implementation of Cilium fully supports its own MCS-API implementation. This is a direct statement of support.

optionRationale.b: EndpointSlice synchronization is mentioned for alternate Gateway-API implementations that rely on EndpointSlice, not for the Cilium Gateway API implementation itself.
optionRationale.c: The Cilium Gateway API implementation supports MCS-API implementations using an underlying Service associated with a ServiceImport and the specific annotation, not those using EndpointSlice.
optionRationale.d: This contradicts the excerpt, which says it fully supports its own MCS-API implementation.

citations.title: Gateway-API
citations.quote: The Gateway API implementation of Cilium fully support its own MCS-API implementation.

questions.stem: You are using an alternate Gateway API implementation with Cilium's MCS-API implementation. What is a prerequisite for this to work, according to the excerpt?

options.text: The Gateway API implementation should officially support MCS-API / GEP1748.
The Gateway API implementation must be Cilium's own implementation.
The ServiceImport must have the annotation `multicluster.kubernetes.io/derived-service`.
The Gateway API implementation must rely on EndpointSlice.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if you want to use another Gateway API implementation with the Cilium MCS-API implementation, the Gateway API implementation you are using should officially support MCS-API / GEP1748. This is the stated prerequisite.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly discusses using another Gateway API implementation, so it does not have to be Cilium's own.
optionRationale.c: The annotation requirement is specific to the Cilium Gateway API implementation, not a general prerequisite for alternate implementations.
optionRationale.d: Relying on EndpointSlice is a characteristic that may require additional configuration, but it is not a prerequisite; the prerequisite is official support for MCS-API.

citations.title: Gateway-API
citations.quote:
If you want to use another Gateway API implementation with the Cilium MCS-API implementation,

questions.stem: An operator is running with an external IPAM plugin, and the platform team wants to alert on how long calls to that external IPAM API take, broken down by the operation performed and the response code returned. Which cilium-operator metric should the alert be built on?

`ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`

questions.explanation: `ipam_api_duration_seconds` is the metric described as the duration of interactions with the external IPAM API, and it carries the `operation` and `response_code` labels, which is exactly the breakdown the team needs.

optionRationale.b: ``ipam_resync_total`` counts synchronization operations with the external IPAM API; it is a count, not a duration, and carries no ``response_code`` label.
optionRationale.c: ``ipam_api_rate_limit_duration_seconds`` measures time spent rate limiting while accessing the external IPAM API, not the duration of the API interactions themselves, and its only label is ``operation``.
optionRationale.d: ``ipam_allocation_duration_seconds`` measures allocation latency and is labelled by ``type``, ``status`` and ``subnet_id``, not by ``operation`` and ``response_code``.

questions.stem: A platform team runs a microservices cluster in which pods are created and destroyed constantly during rolling updates. They currently secure traffic with iptables rules that match on IP addresses and TCP/UDP ports. What problem does the excerpt identify with this approach?

options.text: IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic microservices environments, so filtering on them struggles to scale alongside the application.
iptables cannot be loaded on modern Linux kernels once eBPF has been enabled on the node.
iptables rules can only match on HTTP headers, which the team is not yet using.
iptables requires the application to be modified so that it exposes its identity to the kernel.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that traditional approaches such as iptables filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, but IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic microservices environments, and the highly volatile container life cycle causes these approaches to struggle to scale side by side with the application.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt never says iptables cannot run alongside eBPF; it criticises the filtering model, not kernel compatibility.
optionRationale.c: The opposite is true: the excerpt says traditional approaches filter on IP address and TCP/UDP ports, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says eBPF works transparently without requiring the application to change in any way; it does not attribute an application-modification requirement to iptables.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
Traditional Linux network security approaches (e.g., iptables) filter on IP
address and TCP/UDP ports, but IP addresses frequently churn in dynamic
microservices environments.

questions.stem: A security architect wants to distinguish between different kinds of application traffic between services, but finds that TCP port 80 carries a wide range of messages across those services. According to the excerpt, what does Cilium offer in this situation?

options.text: It can filter on application-layer protocols such as HTTP, in addition to providing traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.
It reassigns each service to a dedicated TCP port so that port-based rules become meaningful again.
It replaces TCP with a proprietary transport that carries identity information in every packet.
It restricts security enforcement to Layer 3 and Layer 4 only, leaving application traffic unclassified.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that protocol ports can no longer differentiate application traffic for security purposes, and that Cilium can filter on application-layer (e.g. HTTP), providing stronger security isolation by operating at the HTTP layer in addition to traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not describe port reassignment; it says ports can no longer be used to differentiate application traffic.
optionRationale.c: No proprietary transport is mentioned; the excerpt refers to lightweight protocols like HTTP and to filtering on application-layer.
optionRationale.d: This inverts the excerpt, which says Cilium operates at the HTTP layer in addition to Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
can filter on application-layer (e.g. HTTP).  As a
result, Cilium not only makes it simple to apply security policies in a highly
dynamic environment by decoupling security from addressing, but can also
provide stronger security isolation by operating at the HTTP-layer in addition
to providing traditional Layer 3 and Layer 4 segmentation.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, on what basis does Cilium insert security visibility and enforcement, in contrast to traditional systems?

options.text: On service, pod or container identity rather than IP address identification.
On the IP address of the node hosting each container.
On the TCP or UDP port number used by each service.
On the MAC address of each virtual network interface.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that Cilium retains the ability to transparently insert security visibility and enforcement, but does so based on service / pod / container identity, in contrast to IP address identification in traditional systems.

optionRationale.b: Node IP addresses are still IP-based identification, which the excerpt contrasts with Cilium's identity-based approach.
optionRationale.c: Port-based differentiation is the traditional model the excerpt says no longer works for application traffic.
optionRationale.d: MAC addresses are not mentioned anywhere in the excerpt.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
By leveraging Linux eBPF, Cilium retains the ability to transparently insert
security visibility + enforcement, but does so in a way that is based on
service / pod / container identity (in contrast to IP address identification in
traditional systems)

questions.stem: An operations team is concerned that adopting eBPF-based networking will require developers to rewrite their applications. What does the excerpt say about this?

options.text: eBPF provides visibility and control in a completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any way.
Applications must be recompiled against the eBPF libraries before Cilium can observe them.
Only containerised workloads can be observed, so virtual machines must be migrated first.
Applications must expose a sidecar API so that eBPF programs can query their state.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says eBPF enables visibility into and control over systems and applications at a granularity and efficiency not possible before, and does so in a completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any way.

optionRationale.b: Recompilation is not mentioned; the excerpt stresses that no application change is required.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle containerised workloads as well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.
optionRationale.d: No sidecar API is described; the mechanism is described as transparent.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
It does so in a
completely transparent way, without requiring the application to change in any
way.

questions.stem: Which statement about the range of workloads eBPF can handle is supported by the excerpt?

options.text: It is equally well-equipped for modern containerised workloads and for more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.
It is designed exclusively for containerised workloads and cannot observe virtual machines.
It supports virtual machines only when they run a container runtime inside them.
It supports standard Linux processes only after they are placed in a Kubernetes pod.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle modern containerised workloads as well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux processes.

optionRationale.b: This contradicts the explicit mention of virtual machines and standard Linux processes as supported workloads.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt places no such condition on virtual machine support.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt mentions standard Linux processes directly, with no requirement for a Kubernetes pod.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?

eBPF is equally well-equipped to handle modern containerized workloads as
well as more traditional workloads such as virtual machines and standard Linux
processes.

questions.stem: A team worries that identity-based security enforcement will not cope as their microservices environment grows very large. What does the excerpt say about scalability?

options.text: The use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve this in a way that is highly scalable even for large-scale environments.
Scalability is achieved only by sharding the cluster into many small clusters.
Scalability depends on keeping access control lists below a fixed rule count.
Scalability is limited because identity lookups must be performed by an external database.

questions.explanation: The excerpt closes by stating that the use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve all of this in a way that is highly scalable even for large-scale environments.

optionRationale.b: Cluster sharding is not mentioned in the excerpt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt mentions hundreds of thousands of rules only as a burden on traditional approaches, not as a limit on Cilium.
optionRationale.d: No external identity database is described in the excerpt.

citations.title: Why Cilium & Hubble?
citations.quote:
The use of eBPF enables Cilium to achieve all of this in a way that is highly
scalable even for large-scale environments.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed in the excerpt as a reason why a root-privilege host attacker may have full privileges on the local host?

options.text: Pods running with `privileged: true` or significant capabilities such as `CAP_BPF`, `CAP_NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_NET_RAW`, or `CAP_SYS_ADMIN`.
Pods running with a read-only root filesystem and no added capabilities.
A CiliumNetworkPolicy that selects the host namespace.
Enabling the cilium-operator's service account in a different namespace.

optionRationale.b: A read-only root filesystem with no added capabilities is not mentioned as a source of root-equivalent access.
optionRationale.c: CiliumNetworkPolicy is not mentioned in the excerpt at all.
optionRationale.d: The operator service account is discussed as an attack vector once the node is compromised, not as a cause of root access.

questions.stem: You have configured the native routing CIDR correctly across your clusters, but pods in one cluster still cannot reach pods in another. Establishing peering or VPN tunnels between the networks of the nodes of each cluster.
Allowing all ports between the node networks with firewall rules.
Allocating all cluster CIDRs from the 10.0.0.0/8 private address space.
