questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium in kvstore/etcd mode and the kvstore becomes unavailable. An engineer asks whether existing pods will keep having their network policy enforced. What does the excerpt say?

options.text: Policy enforcement for existing workloads/endpoints continues, because datapath operations do not depend on the kvstore.
Policy enforcement stops for all endpoints until the kvstore returns, because policy rules are read from etcd on every packet.
Policy enforcement continues only for endpoints whose security identity was allocated after the outage began.
Policy enforcement is suspended only for layer 7 policies, while layer 3 and layer 4 rules continue.

questions.explanation: The excerpt lists all datapath operations among the operations which do not require kvstore availability, stating that packets continue to be forwarded and network policy rules continue to be enforced for existing workloads/endpoints.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: datapath forwarding, policy enforcement and visibility for existing workloads/endpoints do not depend on the kvstore.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no such distinction by allocation time; it says all datapath operations for existing workloads/endpoints are unaffected.
optionRationale.d: Layer 7 proxies are mentioned only as possibly briefly unavailable if the agent must restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior, not as a policy-enforcement suspension.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
All datapath forwarding, policy enforcement and visibility functions for
existing workloads/endpoints do not depend on the kvstore.

questions.stem: In an etcd-mode cluster, a new workload is scheduled onto a node and it re-uses a security identity that is already known. What does the excerpt warn may still happen?

options.text: Nothing is affected, because re-using a known identity removes all kvstore dependency for that endpoint.
Packet drops due to policy enforcement may be observed, because state propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes still depends on the kvstore.
The endpoint will be assigned a new security identity by the kvstore before any traffic is allowed.
The workload will be rescheduled to another node until the kvstore is reachable.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that even when a workload can be scheduled by re-using a known security identity, propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes still depends on the kvstore, so packet drops due to policy enforcement may be observed because other nodes are unaware of the new workload.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt explicitly says state propagation to other nodes still depends on the kvstore despite identity re-use.
optionRationale.c: Identity re-use is described as avoiding the need for a new allocation; the excerpt does not say a new identity is assigned.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes packet drops due to policy enforcement, not rescheduling of the workload.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
If a
  workload can be scheduled due to re-using a known security identity, then
  state propagation of the endpoint details to other nodes will still depend on
  the kvstore

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed in the excerpt as an operation for which the kvstore is strictly required when running in etcd mode?

options.text: Forwarding of packets for existing endpoints
Application of network policy updates
Registration of new nodes in the kvstore
Processing of updates to services

questions.explanation: Node discovery is listed under the operations for which the kvstore is strictly required: new nodes must register themselves in the kvstore.

optionRationale.a: Forwarding for existing endpoints is listed under operations which do not require kvstore availability.
optionRationale.b: Network policy updates are listed as continuing to be processed and applied without the kvstore.
optionRationale.d: Services updates are listed under operations which do not require kvstore availability.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Node discovery:
  New nodes require to register themselves in the kvstore.

questions.stem: A Cilium agent in etcd mode starts up while the kvstore is unreachable. According to the excerpt, how does the agent behave?

options.text: It exits immediately without performing any operations until the kvstore appears.
It eventually fails, but still performs all possible operations while waiting for the kvstore to appear.
It falls back to CRD-mode automatically and continues indefinitely.
It blocks all datapath programming on its node until the kvstore connection succeeds.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the agent will eventually fail if it cannot connect to the kvstore at bootstrap time, but it will still perform all possible operations while waiting for the kvstore to appear.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the agent still performs all possible operations while waiting, so it does not simply exit without doing anything.
optionRationale.c: No automatic fallback to CRD-mode is described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: Datapath operations are listed as not requiring the kvstore, so blocking them is not what the excerpt describes.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
The Cilium agent will eventually fail if it can't connect to the kvstore at
  bootstrap time, however, the agent will still perform all possible operations
  while waiting for the kvstore to appear.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the difference between CRD-mode and kvstore/etcd mode as described in the excerpt?

options.text: In kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore becomes a vital component of overall cluster health, required to be available for several operations.
In CRD-mode the kvstore is still required, but only for multi-cluster state propagation.
In kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore is optional and only used for visibility functions.
Both modes require the kvstore equally; the only difference is where the CRDs are stored.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says Cilium can run in CRD-mode and kvstore/etcd mode, and that in kvstore/etcd mode the kvstore becomes a vital component of overall cluster health because it must be available for several operations.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the kvstore is required in CRD-mode; the kvstore requirements described apply when running in etcd mode.
optionRationale.c: The kvstore is described as vital in etcd mode, and visibility functions are listed among operations that do not depend on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt distinguishes the modes and attaches the kvstore dependency to kvstore/etcd mode, not to both equally.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
When cilium is
running in kvstore/etcd mode, the kvstore becomes a vital component of the
overall cluster health as it is required to be available for several
operations.

questions.stem: An operator notes that the Cilium agent had to restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior. According to the excerpt, what delays can this cause?

options.text: Permanent loss of all existing endpoints on the node.
Delays in processing of flow events and metrics, and short unavailability of layer 7 proxies.
Delays in applying network policy updates and service updates.
Delays in registering new nodes in the kvstore.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that if the agent requires to restart as part of the etcd_recovery_behavior, there can be delays in processing of flow events and metrics, and short unavailability of layer 7 proxies.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt mentions only delays and short unavailability, not permanent loss of endpoints.
optionRationale.c: Network policy updates and services updates are listed as continuing to be processed and applied, not as delayed by the restart.
optionRationale.d: Node registration is a kvstore-required operation, but the excerpt does not attribute delays in it to the agent restart.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
However, if the agent requires to restart as part of the
  etcd_recovery_behavior, there can be delays in:

  * processing of flow events and metrics
  * short unavailability of layer 7 proxies

questions.stem: A platform team runs a cluster whose nodes are on Linux 5.15 and wants to enable BBR congestion control for Pods through Cilium's bandwidth manager. What does the excerpt say about this plan?

options.text: It will work, but only for Pods that stay in the host network namespace.
It will not work reliably, because BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel.
It will work as long as eBPF Host-Routing is enabled, since the kernel version is irrelevant.
It will work, but only for Pods exposed behind Kubernetes Services.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states plainly that BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel, and repeats that a 5.18 or higher kernel is needed for BBR to work reliably for Pods. A 5.15 kernel therefore does not meet the requirement, and enabling eBPF Host-Routing does not remove the kernel constraint.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says that prior to that kernel, BBR was only working for sockets in the initial network namespace (hostns), which is the opposite of the claim that it would work for Pods there.
optionRationale.c: eBPF Host-Routing is described as an additional requirement, not a substitute for the kernel version; the excerpt explicitly ties reliability to a 5.18 or higher kernel.
optionRationale.d: Being exposed behind Services is given as the situation where BBR is particularly suitable, not as a workaround for an old kernel.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: BBR for Pods requires a v5.18.x or more recent Linux kernel.

questions.stem: An engineer enables the bandwidth manager with BBR on a recent kernel but does not enable eBPF Host-Routing. According to the excerpt, what is the consequence?

options.text: The packet's socket association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer, so BBR cannot retain it until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device.
The kernel would stop retaining timestamps of network packets when switching from Pod to host network namespace.
Cilium would silently fall back to CUBIC for all Pods, and the status line would show EDT with BPF [CUBIC].
BBR would still work, but only for sockets in the initial network namespace.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that BBR needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace, and that without it the association would be orphaned inside the host stack's forwarding/routing layer.

optionRationale.b: The timestamp retention issue is attributed to older kernels, not to the absence of eBPF Host-Routing.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe any automatic fallback to CUBIC or a CUBIC status line.
optionRationale.d: Working only for sockets in the initial network namespace is what the excerpt says about kernels prior to the fix, not about missing eBPF Host-Routing.

citations.title: BBR for Pods
citations.quote: BBR also needs eBPF Host-Routing in order to retain the network packet's socket association all the way until the packet hits the FQ queueing discipline on the physical device in the host namespace.

questions.stem: Which command does the excerpt present for verifying whether the bandwidth manager with BBR has been enabled in Cilium?

options.text: kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager
kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg bpf bandwidth list

questions.stem: An engineer wants Cilium's eBPF NodePort implementation to let backends reply directly to external clients without the extra hop, and also wants policy at the backend node to be able to match on the client's source IP. Which change achieves both goals?

questions.stem: The Cilium Operator becomes temporarily unavailable in a cluster. According to the excerpt, what is the expected effect?

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, and that the two are mutually exclusive. No manual step is required, and the modes cannot run together.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the modes are mutually exclusive, so they cannot both serve traffic at once.

questions.stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service in a cluster that uses kube-proxy, and the backend application must see the original client IP. Which Service setting does the excerpt say is the only way to ensure source IP visibility in this situation?

optionRationale.b: ``Cluster`` is described as allowing the node to masquerade the source IP, so the backend pod may not see it.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that leaving the field unset defaults it to ``Local``; it only describes the two relevant settings.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the ``healthCheckNodePort`` is automatically set by Kubernetes when ``externalTrafficPolicy: Local`` is set, and does not suggest disabling it.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the `Cluster` setting of `externalTrafficPolicy` as presented in the excerpt?

questions.stem: A cluster uses the `multi-pool` IPAM mode. Its `default` `CiliumPodIPPool` currently contains `10.10.0.0/16`, and running pods still hold addresses from that range. The platform team must change the pool to use `10.20.0.0/16`. According to the excerpt, what approach should they use?

options.text: Split the cluster into two node groups and migrate workloads from nodes using the old CIDR to nodes using the new CIDR.
Delete the `CiliumPodIPPool` and immediately recreate it with `10.20.0.0/16`; existing pods will keep working without further action.
Add `10.20.0.0/16` as an additional CIDR and leave `10.10.0.0/16` in place; no workload migration is needed.
Update the in-use CIDR in place and restart only the Cilium operator; pods will receive new addresses on their next restart.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that changing the CIDR of a pool requires re-assigning the IPs of existing workloads. It recommends achieving this by splitting the cluster into two node groups so that workloads can be migrated from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR. The restriction described prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes, so simply recreating or updating the pool in place is not the described approach.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that deleting and recreating the pool lets existing pods keep working without further action; it describes a migration process because existing workloads must be re-assigned IPs.
optionRationale.c: Extending a pool with new CIDRs is possible, but the objective here is to change the existing default pool CIDR, and the excerpt says the restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe updating an in-use CIDR in place as sufficient; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use and gives a node-group migration procedure instead.

into two node groups, which allows you to migrate the workloads from nodes using the old CIDR over to nodes using the new CIDR.

questions.stem: An engineer maintains an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` resource that is already in use by pods. They want to add a new IPv6 CIDR to the pool. Which statement reflects the limitation described in the excerpt?

options.text: They may extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but they cannot delete or update CIDRs already in use.
They may delete an in-use CIDR once the pods using it have been cordoned, because cordoning releases the CIDR from the pool.
They may update an in-use CIDR in place, provided the Cilium operator is restarted first.
They cannot add any new CIDRs to an existing pool; a new `CiliumPodIPPools` resource must always be created.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use. It also explains that this restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that cordoning releases an in-use CIDR from the pool; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not permit updating an in-use CIDR in place after restarting the Cilium operator; it says it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says it is possible to extend the pool by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, so it is not true that no new CIDRs can be added to an existing pool.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote:
It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to
delete or update the CIDRs already in use.

questions.stem: A Kubernetes cluster uses Cilium's egress-gateway with egress IP 10.1.0.0 to masquerade external connections to a server at 10.2.0.0:8080 behind a firewall. The firewall permits only connections whose source IP is 10.1.0.0. Many clients connect to that same remote endpoint, and the connection count for the tuple {10.1.0.0, 10.2.0.0, 8080} is approaching 32768. According to the excerpt, what is the only solution?

options.text: Reduce the number of connections being SNATed through the egress-gateway, for example by having clients create fewer new connections or by splitting traffic across different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses.
Increase the upper bound of --node-port-range so that more source ports become available to the SNAT map.
Add more egress-gateway nodes so that SNAT mappings are distributed across multiple Cilium agents.
Run cilium-dbg shell -- db/show nat-stats more frequently so that the SNAT map is recalculated and capacity is freed.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that because this is a hard limit on Cilium's Egress Gateway functionality, the only solution is to reduce the number of connections being SNATed through an egress-gateway. It suggests having clients avoid creating as many new connections, or lowering the number of connections going to the same remote address with a common egress IP by splitting traffic via different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt defines the limit as the difference between 65535 and the upper bound of --node-port-range; raising that upper bound would not create more source ports, and the excerpt says the only solution is to reduce connections.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not present adding egress-gateway nodes as a solution; it says the problem is a hard limit and the only solution is to reduce the number of SNATed connections.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says these stats are re-calculated every 30 seconds by default; querying them more often does not free SNAT capacity.

citations.title: Example Scenario
citations.quote:
Because this problem is a result of hitting a hard limit on Cilium's Egress Gateway functionality, the only solution is to reduce the number of connections
that are being SNATed through an egress-gateway, This can be done by having clients avoid creating as many new connections, or by lowering the amount of connections going to the same remote address (with a common egress IP) by splitting up traffic via different egress IPs and/or remote endpoint addresses.

questions.stem: Cilium is running with IPsec encryption enabled. While reviewing the Cilium log files, an engineer finds a `level=warning` message reading `Device eth0 does not exist`. What does the excerpt say to do?

options.text: Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.
Increase the delay before old key cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Confirm that the IPsec `Secret` and Cilium are deployed in the same namespace together.

questions.explanation: The excerpt instructs you to check for `level=warning` and `level=error` messages in the Cilium log files, and states that if there is a warning message similar to `Device eth0 does not exist`, you should use `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX` to set the encryption interface. The other options are remedies drawn from unrelated parts of the excerpt: key rotation timing, SPI handling for `XfrmInStateProtoError`, and the namespace check for Pods that fail to start.

optionRationale.b: The ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration`` flag is suggested for lengthening the delay before cleanup when key rotation is expected to take longer, not for a missing device warning.
optionRationale.c: A proper new key rotation is the fix given for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` caused by a key update without an incremented SPI, a different symptom entirely.
optionRationale.d: The namespace check applies when the ``cilium`` Pods fail to start after enabling encryption; here the Pods are running and logging a warning.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If there is a warning message similar to ``Device eth0 does not exist``,
     use ``--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`` to set the encryption
     interface.

questions.stem: A Cluster Mesh deployment spanning several clusters is rotating its IPsec keys. Because every cluster must be updated, the rotation takes considerably longer than usual, and `XfrmInNoStates` errors start appearing. Which action does the excerpt recommend?

options.text: Increase the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.
Perform a new key rotation, properly, so that the SPI is incremented.
Take no action, because `XfrmInNoStates` counters are only expected to rise while a rebooted node's new key is being deployed.
Set the encryption interface with `--set encryption.ipsec.interface=ethX`.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that if the old key is cleaned up before the new key's configuration is installed on all nodes, `XfrmInNoStates` errors result, and that the old key is removed after a default interval of 5 minutes while agents normally update their configuration within 1 minute. Where the rotation is expected to take longer — the excerpt's own example being Cluster Mesh with several clusters to update — it recommends increasing the delay before cleanup with the agent flag `ipsec-key-rotation-duration`.

optionRationale.b: A proper new key rotation is the stated fix for ``XfrmInStateProtoError`` arising from a key update without an incremented SPI, not for slow Cluster Mesh rotation.
optionRationale.c: Rising ``XfrmInNoStates`` counters during a node reboot are indeed expected, but the excerpt separately attributes ``XfrmInNoStates`` to premature cleanup of the old key after a rotation, which is the situation described here.
optionRationale.d: The encryption interface setting addresses a ``Device eth0 does not exist`` warning and has no bearing on key rotation timing.

citations.title: Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
If you expect
   the key rotation to take longer for some reason (for example, in the case of
   Cluster Mesh where several clusters need to be updated), you can increase the
   delay before cleanup with agent flag ``ipsec-key-rotation-duration``.

questions.stem: An engineer has just added service.cilium.io/shared="false" to the rebel-base Service in cluster 1. Before removing the annotation, they run kubectl exec -ti deployment/x-wing -- curl rebel-base from cluster 1. What should they observe?

options.text: Replies from pods in both clusters.
Replies only from pods in cluster 1.
Replies only from pods in cluster 2.
No replies from any pods.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that, after the annotation is added in cluster 1, accessing the global service from cluster 1 still shows replies from pods in both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 1.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says that from cluster 1 the replies still come from both clusters, not only from cluster 2.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says that replies are still seen from pods in both clusters, not that no pods reply.

citations.title: Deploying a Simple Example Service
citations.quote: You will still see replies from pods in both clusters.

questions.stem: A platform engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy under the behaviour described in the excerpt. The egress rule uses toEndpoints with matchLabels name: rebel-base and does not include any cluster label or cluster match expression. Which endpoints will the policy select?

options.text: Endpoints named rebel-base in the local cluster only.
Endpoints named rebel-base in every cluster in the Cluster Mesh.
Endpoints named rebel-base in cluster2 only.
No endpoints, because a cluster label is mandatory for toEndpoints.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only unless one or more clusters are specifically targeted. Therefore, a toEndpoints selector with only name: rebel-base selects local endpoints. The excerpt also notes that in Cilium v1.18 or lower, policies used to select endpoints from all clusters by default, but that is not the behaviour described for the current policy default.

optionRationale.b: Selecting endpoints from all clusters was the default in Cilium v1.18 or lower, not the behaviour described for the current policy default.
optionRationale.c: Targeting cluster2 only requires an explicit cluster label such as io.cilium.k8s.policy.cluster: cluster2.
optionRationale.d: A cluster label is not mandatory; without one, the policy selects endpoints from the local cluster only.

citations.title: Allowing Specific Communication Between Clusters
citations.quote:
Policies automatically select endpoints from the local cluster only, unless one
or multiple cluster are specifically targeted.

questions.stem: A policy contains two `toPorts` entries. Both entries use the same `PortProtocol` and select an overlapping list of endpoints. The first entry defines HTTP layer 7 rules, while the second defines DNS layer 7 rules. What happens?

options.text: The policy is rejected because the layer 7 rule types differ.
The HTTP and DNS rules are combined and both are enforced.
The HTTP rules are kept and the DNS rules are silently ignored.
The DNS rules are kept and the HTTP rules are silently ignored.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that layer 7 rules from multiple `toPorts` entries with the same `PortProtocol` and overlapping endpoints are combined only when they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

optionRationale.b: Combining is permitted only when the layer 7 rules are of the same type; here the types differ.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not describe silently ignoring one type; a type difference causes rejection.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If multiple ``toPorts`` rules with identical ``PortProtocol`` select an overlapping list of endpoints, then the layer 7 rules are combined together if they are of the same type. If the type differs, the policy is rejected.

questions.stem: A policy contains a layer 4 rule for a set of endpoints and also a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules for the same endpoints. What is the effect of the layer 7 portion of the second rule?

options.text: It has no effect.
It is enforced in addition to the first layer 4 rule.
It overrides the first layer 4 rule and permits only matching layer 7 requests.
It causes the policy to be rejected because layer 4 and layer 7 rules cannot coexist.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that when a layer 4 rule is specified and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, the layer 7 portions of the latter rule have no effect.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the layer 7 portions have no effect, not that they are enforced in addition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not describe the layer 7 portion overriding the first layer 4 rule.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not say the policy is rejected; it says the layer 7 portions have no effect.

citations.title: Layer 7 Policies
citations.quote: If a layer 4 rule is specified in the policy, and a similar layer 4 rule with layer 7 rules is also specified, then the layer 7 portions of the latter rule will have no effect.

questions.stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy has been applied that whitelists traffic sent from any pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. A tiefighter pod carrying the label org=empire sends a POST request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing. What is the expected result?

options.text: The request succeeds and returns Ship landed.
The request is blocked because the policy matches endpoint IP addresses rather than pod labels.
The request hangs because Cilium connection tracking permits only reply packets, not the initial request.
The request succeeds only if the xwing pod is also labelled org=empire.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the policy whitelists traffic from pods with label org=empire to deathstar pods with label org=empire, class=deathstar on TCP port 80. It then says that only the tiefighter pods with the label org=empire will succeed, while the xwing pods will be blocked. Therefore the tiefighter request succeeds and returns Ship landed.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies; matching is by pod labels.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes stateful connection tracking as automatically allowing required reply packets; it does not say the initial request is blocked.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says xwing pods will be blocked; the tiefighter request succeeds because the source pod has org=empire, not because xwing is labelled.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: Now if we run the landing requests again, only the *tiefighter* pods with the label ``org=empire`` will succeed. The *xwing* pods will be blocked!

questions.stem: An engineer is writing a CiliumNetworkPolicy for pods that may be rescheduled to different nodes. They are deciding whether to select the pods by endpoint IP address or by pod label. What does the excerpt say they should do?

options.text: Use endpoint IP addresses, because they remain stable when pods are rescheduled.
Use the labels assigned to the pods, because endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant and policies are applied based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running.
Use the deathstar service DNS name, because Cilium policies match on service names rather than pod identity.
Use both endpoint IP addresses and pod labels, because Cilium requires an IP address in every policy rule.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies and that labels assigned to pods should be used instead. It adds that policies are applied to the right pods based on labels irrespective of where or when the pod is running within the cluster.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies, not stable selection keys.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt discusses pod labels and endpoint IP addresses; it does not say policies match on service DNS names.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to use labels instead of endpoint IP addresses; it does not require both.

citations.title: Apply an L3/L4 Policy
citations.quote: When using Cilium, endpoint IP addresses are irrelevant when defining security policies. Instead, you can use the labels assigned to the pods to define security policies.

questions.stem: An engineer has run the first peering command from the excerpt, creating a peering from cluster one's virtual network to cluster two's virtual network with --allow-vnet-access. Traffic flows from cluster one to cluster two, but traffic originating in cluster two never reaches cluster one. What does the excerpt say is required to fix this?

options.text: Add a peering in the other direction as well, creating a peering from cluster two's virtual network to cluster one's virtual network.
Re-run the same peering command against cluster one's virtual network a second time, because a peering must be applied twice to the same virtual network.
Edit the existing peering so that its --remote-vnet points at cluster one's virtual network instead of cluster two's.
Nothing further is needed: a single peering created with --allow-vnet-access already carries traffic in both directions.

questions.explanation: A single peering only permits outbound traffic from the virtual network in which it is created — in this case from cluster one to cluster two. The excerpt states that to allow bi-directional traffic you must add a peering to the other direction as well, so a second peering has to be created from cluster two's virtual network to cluster one's virtual network.

optionRationale.b: Re-running the same command against the same virtual network does not create the reverse direction; the excerpt calls for a peering in the other direction, not a repeat of the first one.
optionRationale.c: The existing peering is the one that already carries outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two; repointing its --remote-vnet would not add the missing direction described in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says that the first peering allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two and that bi-directional traffic requires a peering in the other direction as well.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
This allows outbound traffic from cluster one to cluster two. To allow
bi-directional traffic, add a peering to the other direction as well.

questions.stem: An engineer is preparing the second peering command, the one that creates the peering from cluster two to cluster one. Before running az network vnet peering create, the engineer must populate the VNET_ID variable. Which value does the excerpt assign to VNET_ID for this command?

options.text: The ID of cluster one's virtual network, queried from the resource group "${CLUSTER1}-group" and the virtual network "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net".
The ID of cluster two's virtual network, queried from the resource group "${CLUSTER2}-group" and the virtual network "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net".
The name of cluster one's virtual network rather than its ID, taken from the --name argument.
The name of cluster one's resource group, taken from the --resource-group argument.

questions.explanation: In the second command block the VNET_ID variable is populated by querying the virtual network in "${CLUSTER1}-group" named "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net", and that value is then passed to --remote-vnet when the peering is created in "${CLUSTER2}-group". The remote virtual network for the reverse peering is therefore cluster one's virtual network.

optionRationale.b: Cluster two's virtual network is the one the peering is created in (--vnet-name "${CLUSTER2}-cluster-net"); it is not the remote virtual network referenced by VNET_ID in this block.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt queries the ID with --query id -o tsv, so the variable holds the ID rather than the name.
optionRationale.d: The resource group is used to locate the virtual network in the az network vnet show command; the value assigned to VNET_ID is the virtual network's ID.

citations.title: Peering virtual networks
citations.quote:
export VNET_ID=$(az network vnet show \
     --resource-group "${CLUSTER1}-group" \
     --name "${CLUSTER1}-cluster-net" \
     --query id -o tsv)

questions.stem: A platform team has installed Cilium with the host firewall enabled and applied a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector to select a group of worker nodes. On one of those selected nodes, two workloads send traffic to destinations outside the cluster: pod A runs with hostNetwork: true, while pod B runs in its own pod network namespace. How does the host policy treat these two flows?

options.text: Both flows are covered, because the policy selects the node on which both pods are running.
Pod A's traffic is covered, because host policies apply to the host namespace including host-networking pods; pod B's traffic to a location outside the cluster is not covered.
Neither flow is covered, because host policies apply only to the node's own host namespace and never to any pod.
Only pod B's traffic is covered, because host policies explicitly exclude host-networking pods from the host namespace.

questions.explanation: A host policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy that uses a NodeSelector, and it applies to all the nodes that selector picks. Within each selected node, however, its scope is the host namespace, which expressly includes host-networking pods. Communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside the cluster fall outside that scope, so pod B's flow is not governed by the host policy even though its node is selected.

optionRationale.a: Selecting the node is necessary but not sufficient: the policy's scope inside the node is the host namespace, so a pod in its own network namespace sending traffic outside the cluster is not covered.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host policies apply to the host namespace 'including host-networking pods', so host-networking pod traffic is covered rather than excluded.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the opposite: host-networking pods are included in the host namespace, and it is non-host-networking pods talking to locations outside the cluster that are excluded.

citations.title: Host Policies
citations.quote: Host policies apply to all the nodes selected by their NodeSelector. In each selected node, they apply only to the host namespace, including host-networking pods. They don't apply to communications between non-host-networking pods and locations outside of the cluster.

questions.stem: An engineer has a LoadBalancer Service with spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges populated. By default the CIDR restrictions apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the NodePort and ClusterIP services created alongside it. The engineer wants those CIDRs to filter traffic for all externally exposed service types as well. Which action does the excerpt describe for this?

options.text: Enable bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true in Helm.
Add the annotation service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer to the Service.
Set service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny.
Remove spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges so that no restrictions are applied.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says that by default the white-listed CIDRs in spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges apply only to the LoadBalancer service, not to the corresponding NodePort or ClusterIP service. It then states that propagating the white-listed CIDRs to all externally exposed service types can be enabled in Helm via bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true.

optionRationale.b: The service.cilium.io/type: LoadBalancer annotation is described as a way to avoid the creation of corresponding NodePort and ClusterIP services, not as a way to propagate the CIDRs to them.
optionRationale.c: Setting service.cilium.io/src-ranges-policy to deny turns the CIDR list into a deny-list; it does not propagate the list to the other service types.
optionRationale.d: Removing spec.loadBalancerSourceRanges would leave the field empty, and the excerpt says that if the field is empty, no restrictions for the access will be applied.

citations.title: LoadBalancer Source Ranges Checks
citations.quote: This option can be enabled in Helm via ``bpf.lbSourceRangeAllTypes=true``.

questions.stem: You are troubleshooting an Ingress connectivity problem and want to enable the Cilium debugging flags recommended in the excerpt. What must you do for the change to take effect?

options.text: Restart the Cilium agent and operator.
Restart only the Cilium Envoy proxy pods.
Recreate the affected Ingress resource.
No restart is needed; the flags are read dynamically.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that any change of Cilium flags requires a restart of the Cilium agent and operator, so enabling `debug` and `debug-verbose` will not take effect until both are restarted.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the Cilium agent and operator, not the Envoy proxy pods, as the components needing a restart.
optionRationale.c: Recreating the Ingress is not mentioned as a way to apply flag changes.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says a restart is required, so dynamic pickup is wrong.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
Kindly
note that any change of Cilium flags requires a restart of the Cilium agent and operator.

questions.stem: When checking the Envoy Discovery Service for a backend, what naming convention does the EDS name follow?

options.text: `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>`
`<service-name>.<namespace>:<port>`
`cilium-ingress-<namespace>-<service-name>`
`<namespace>-<service-name>-<port>`

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Envoy Discovery Service (EDS) has a name that follows the convention `<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>`, as seen in the example names `default/details:9080` and `default/productpage:9080`.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the separator and ordering; the excerpt uses a slash between namespace and service name.
optionRationale.c: This resembles the proxy port name pattern seen in the logs, not the EDS naming convention.
optionRationale.d: This uses hyphens throughout, which does not match the stated convention.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
The Envoy Discovery Service
    (EDS) has a name that follows the convention ``<namespace>/<service-name>:<port>``.

questions.stem: You send a request through the external IP of your Ingress and receive the response `no healthy upstream`. According to the excerpt, what should you double-check?

options.text: Whether your backend service is up and healthy.
Whether the cloud Load Balancer is configured properly.
Whether the `debug-verbose` flag is set to `flow`.
Whether the Cilium operator is running.

questions.explanation: After the earlier steps succeed and you send a request via an external IP or FQDN, the excerpt advises double-checking whether your backend service is up and healthy, which is the situation illustrated by the `no healthy upstream` response.

optionRationale.b: The LoadBalancer-to-node-port step is out of Cilium scope and is checked earlier in the sequence, not in response to `no healthy upstream`.
optionRationale.c: The debug flags are recommended for troubleshooting generally, but the excerpt does not tie this response to them.
optionRationale.d: The operator is mentioned only in connection with restarting after flag changes.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote: Double-check whether your backend service is up and healthy.

questions.stem: Which command does the excerpt show for observing flows for the world identity while troubleshooting?

options.text: `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- hubble observe -f --identity 2`
`kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status`
`kubectl logs -f -n kube-system ds/cilium --timestamps`
`kubectl get -n kube-system cm cilium-config -o json`

questions.explanation: The excerpt labels the command `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- hubble observe -f --identity 2` as the one for flows for world identity.

optionRationale.b: This command is shown for checking controller and proxy status, not for observing flows.
optionRationale.c: This command is shown for finding proxy port log messages.
optionRationale.d: This command is shown for checking the debug flags in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
# Flows for world identity
     $ kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- hubble observe -f --identity 2

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, what is the most common root cause when a request reaches the proxy but the setup still fails?

options.text: The Cilium Envoy proxy is not running on the node, or there is some other issue with CEC resource provisioning.
The originating source IP is not being used for enforcing ingress traffic.
The `debug` flag has not been set to `true` in the `cilium-config` ConfigMap.
The backend service is exposing the wrong port in its EDS name.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the most common root cause is either that the Cilium Envoy proxy is not running on the node, or there is some other issue with CEC resource provisioning.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt notes that the originating source IP is used for enforcing ingress traffic, but does not present this as a root cause of failure.
optionRationale.c: Debug flags are recommended for troubleshooting but are not named as the root cause.
optionRationale.d: The EDS naming convention is described for checking backend health, not as the most common root cause.

citations.title: Connectivity Troubleshooting
citations.quote:
The most common root cause is either that the Cilium Envoy proxy is not running
on the node, or there is some other issue with CEC resource provisioning.

questions.stem: A platform team is rolling out Cilium on a new cluster and wants Pod-level rate limiting in place from the start. What is the default state of the bandwidth manager on a fresh installation, and what must they do?

options.text: It is enabled by default, so no action is needed beyond annotating Pods.
It is disabled by default on new installations, so Cilium must be installed with the bandwidth manager enabled.
It is enabled by default only when BPF Host Routing is also enabled.
It is disabled by default and can only be turned on by chaining the bandwidth CNI plugin.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations, and that to install Cilium with it enabled you must install Cilium with the bandwidth manager enabled. Nothing in the excerpt makes it conditional on BPF Host Routing, and the bandwidth manager explicitly does not use CNI chaining.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt says the opposite: it is disabled by default on new installations.
optionRationale.c: BPF Host Routing is strongly recommended as a companion, but the excerpt does not make the default enablement conditional on it.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the bandwidth manager does not rely on CNI chaining and does not use the bandwidth CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote: Cilium's bandwidth manager is disabled by default on new installations.

questions.stem: An engineer is asked why Cilium's bandwidth manager does not simply use the Kubernetes bandwidth CNI plugin. Which explanation matches the excerpt?

options.text: The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on EDT, which is less scalable than the TBF approach Cilium uses.
The bandwidth CNI plugin cannot be used with Kubernetes Pod annotations at all.
The bandwidth CNI plugin is based on TBF rather than EDT, and there are scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces.
The bandwidth CNI plugin only works in tunneling mode, whereas Cilium needs direct routing.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the bandwidth manager is natively integrated into Cilium and does not make use of the bandwidth CNI plugin, because of scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network interfaces; that plugin is based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

optionRationale.a: The comparison is inverted: the CNI plugin uses TBF, while Cilium uses EDT.
optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say the CNI plugin is incompatible with annotations; its stated reason is scalability and its TBF basis.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says bandwidth enforcement is supported for direct routing as well as tunneling mode, and gives no such limitation for the CNI plugin.

citations.title: Bandwidth Manager
citations.quote:
Due to scalability concerns in particular for multi-queue network
interfaces, it is not recommended to use the bandwidth CNI plugin which is
based on TBF (Token Bucket Filter) instead of EDT.

questions.stem: A Pod carries both `kubernetes.io/egress-bandwidth` and `kubernetes.io/ingress-bandwidth` annotations. According to the excerpt, how is each direction enforced?

questions.stem: You have a cluster running Cilium and Istio ambient mode. You deploy web servers and clients across the red, blue and green namespaces, then run connectivity checks from each client to httpbin.red and httpbin.blue before applying any policy. What result should you expect?

options.text: All six checks return 200, because Istio's default PERMISSIVE mode allows both ambient-managed and unmanaged pods to exchange unsecured traffic.
Only the checks from red succeed, because the red namespace is the only one enrolled in the ambient mesh by default.
The checks to httpbin.blue fail with exit code 28, because the blue namespace is not part of the ambient mesh.
All six checks return 403, because Cilium's L7 proxy intercepts HTTP traffic before Istio can allow it.

questions.explanation: With no policy applied, Istio operates in PERMISSIVE mode by default, so ambient-managed and unmanaged pods can send and receive unsecured traffic between each other. The excerpt states that all the listed commands should complete successfully, with every check returning 200.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt gives no indication that only the red namespace is enrolled; all six checks are expected to succeed.
optionRationale.c: The 000 result with exit code 28 appears only after the L4 policy restricting the blue namespace is applied, not in the initial run.
optionRationale.d: The 403 response appears only when testing the /deny path after Cilium is enforcing an L7 policy, not in the initial connectivity checks.

optionRationale.c: A 403 response is associated with the later L7 policy test against the /deny path, not with the L4 policy.
optionRationale.d: Only the green client is outside the permitted namespaces, so the other checks still succeed.

questions.stem: A platform team has a global service in cluster 1 with `service.cilium.io/affinity` set to `local`. All local backends in cluster 1 are healthy. A client in cluster 1 curls the global service. What does it observe?

options.text: Replies come only from pods in cluster 1, because the local endpoints are preferred while they remain available and healthy.
Replies come from pods in both clusters, because the affinity annotation only affects endpoints in the remote cluster.
Replies come only from pods in cluster 2, because `local` means the local cluster is excluded from load-balancing.
Replies alternate strictly between cluster 1 and cluster 2, because `local` enables round-robin across clusters.

questions.explanation: With the annotation value `local`, the Global Service load-balances across healthy local backends and only uses remote endpoints if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy. The excerpt's step 2 confirms that from cluster 1 you will see replies from pods in cluster 1 only.

optionRationale.b: The annotation does affect which endpoints are preferred; the excerpt shows cluster 1 clients getting replies from cluster 1 only, not from both clusters.
optionRationale.c: `local` prefers endpoints from the local cluster, not the remote one; `remote` is the value that prefers remote endpoints.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes round-robin alternation between clusters; `local` is a preference for local endpoints, not an interleaving policy.

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium alongside Istio in ambient mode. They want Cilium L7 HTTP policy to govern traffic for a particular workload, but that workload is currently enrolled in Istio ambient. What must they do so that Cilium can enforce L7 policy on that workload's traffic?

options.text: Remove the workload from Istio ambient, either by removing the `istio.io/dataplane-mode` label from the namespace or by annotating the pods with `ambient.istio.io/redirection: disabled`.
Set `mtls.mode=DISABLE` in an Istio PeerAuthentication resource for that workload.
Leave the workload in ambient mode but enable Cilium L7 policy, since Cilium can inspect traffic tunneled over port 15008.

Otherwise Istio encrypts the traffic with mTLS and Cilium cannot access it for L7 policy enforcement. Disabling mTLS via PeerAuthentication is the sidecar-mode remedy, not the ambient one.

optionRationale.b: ``mtls.mode=DISABLE`` under PeerAuthentication is the instruction given for sidecar mode, not for ambient mode.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that traffic tunneled and encrypted by Istio over port 15008 gives Cilium no visibility into source, destination or any L7 information, so leaving the workload in ambient does not work.

questions.stem: An engineer exposes Cilium's Envoy DaemonSet through a NodePort Service and wants the backend Pod to see the client's original address. She is using Cilium Ingress and is deciding whether she must set `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` on that Service. What does the excerpt say about this requirement?

options.text: It is not necessary, because Cilium ingress traffic is always sent to the local node and forwarded to Envoy via TPROXY, keeping the source IP visible through `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address`.
It is mandatory, because only `Local` prevents masquerading of the source IP for any Service that exposes Envoy.
It is mandatory, because `Cluster` causes the node to always masquerade the source IP for ingress traffic.
It is not necessary, because Cilium rewrites the source IP into the `healthCheckNodePort` response headers instead.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that for Cilium's ingress config, both Ingress and Gateway API, it is not necessary to configure `externalTrafficPolicy: Local` to keep the source IP visible to the backend pod, via the `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Envoy-External-Address` fields. A request to `http://<nodeIP>:<healthCheckNodePort>/healthz` returns non-200 on nodes with local Pods and 200 on nodes without them.
No such port is opened; the operator must inspect EndpointSlices to determine local Pod presence.

`Local` and `Cluster` differ only in the health check port number that Kubernetes assigns automatically.

questions.stem: An engineer sees `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors on a node. Which two situations are documented as causes?

options.text: The key was updated without incrementing the SPI, or the source node encrypts using a different anti-replay seq from the anti-reply oseq on the destination node
A packet was received while an XFRM state was being deleted, or the kernel failed to route a packet for a deleted pod
The kernel failed to allocate memory, or the sequence number of an encryption XFRM configuration reached its maximum value
Cilium dropped packets that would otherwise have left the node in plain-text, or the destination node's IP address changed

questions.explanation: `XfrmInStateProtoError` errors can happen if the key is updated without incrementing the SPI (also called `KEYID`), or if the source node encrypts the packets using a different anti-replay seq from the anti-reply oseq on the destination node. optionRationale.b: These describe `XfrmInStateInvalid` and `XfrmFwdHdrError`/`XfrmInError` respectively.
optionRationale.c: These describe `XfrmFwdHdrError`/`XfrmInError` and `XfrmOutStateSeqError` respectively.
optionRationale.d: These describe `XfrmOutPolBlock` and the `No node ID found` drops respectively.

questions.stem: A Cilium-managed pod on a node is the source of a TCP connection. The connection completes its handshake and moves into the ESTABLISHED state, and the peer is a node-local process. Which behaviour does Cilium exhibit at that moment?

options.text: The socket operations program, attached to the root cgroup, detects the ESTABLISHED transition and, because the socket has a node local peer, attaches a socket send/recv program to the socket.
The XDP program attached to the container's veth pair drops the packet so that the connection must be re-established through the proxy.
The L3 Encryption object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and marks the socket for encryption before any further processing.
The Service object performs a map lookup on the destination IP and port and forwards the packet to one of the configured L3/L4 endpoints.

questions.explanation: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup and uses it to monitor TCP state transitions, specifically ESTABLISHED. When a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED and the TCP socket has a node local peer (possibly a local proxy), a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: XDP runs at the earliest point in the networking driver on packet reception and is used for filtering such as dropping malicious traffic; it is not what reacts to a TCP state transition on an established socket.
optionRationale.c: The L3 Encryption object's map lookup on the destination IP happens on egress to decide whether a packet should be encrypted; it is not triggered by a socket entering ESTABLISHED.
optionRationale.d: The Service object does a map lookup on destination IP and optionally port for packets received by that object and forwards to L3/L4 endpoints; it is not the component that attaches a program on an ESTABLISHED transition.

questions.explanation: The **. prefix is a special wildcard that matches all cascaded subdomains in the prefix. Therefore **.cilium.io matches both app.cilium.io and test.app.cilium.io, but not cilium.io itself.

optionRationale.b: The **.cilium.io pattern does not match cilium.io, because the wildcard covers subdomains only.
optionRationale.c: The pattern is anchored to the cilium.io suffix, so a name with cilium.io as a leading label does not match.
optionRationale.d: The pattern requires the cilium.io suffix, so a name ending in cilium.com does not match.

questions.stem: In a Cilium TLS inspection setup, which statement best describes the role of the internal certificate authority?

options.text: It is an entity trusted to create proof that a given network service is who it claims to be, and it signs certificates for external destinations so that Cilium can act as those destinations.
It is a public certificate authority that automatically issues certificates for any destination without additional configuration.
It is a component that stores private keys for individual destination services as Kubernetes secrets.
It is a mechanism that encrypts all traffic between Cilium and the destination service without terminating TLS.

questions.explanation: The excerpt defines a Certificate Authority as 'an entity that is trusted to create proof that a given network service (e.g., www.cilium.io) is who they say they are.' In the friendly interception model, the network security team creates their own internal certificate authority to create alternative certificates for external destinations. Cilium then uses a certificate signed by this internal CA to act like the destination service and terminate the TLS connection.

optionRationale.b: The internal CA is created by the network security team, not a public authority, and it is used for specific destinations where inspection is desired.
optionRationale.c: Private keys for individual destination services are stored as Kubernetes secrets, but that is separate from the CA's role.
optionRationale.d: Cilium terminates the TLS connection and initiates a new one; it does not merely encrypt traffic without termination.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: the network security team creates their own "internal certificate authority" that can be used to create alternative certificates for external destinations.

questions.stem: How does the TLS inspection model used by Cilium for network security monitoring differ from the standard TLS authentication model?

options.text: In the standard model, a trusted certificate authority proves the identity of the destination service; in the Cilium inspection model, the network security team creates an internal CA to issue alternative certificates for external destinations, which clients must trust.
In the standard model, clients do not verify certificates; in the Cilium inspection model, clients verify certificates against the internal CA.
In the standard model, the destination service signs its own certificates; in the Cilium inspection model, the client signs certificates for the destination.
In the standard model, a public CA is always used; in the Cilium inspection model, the internal CA is optional and only used for logging.

questions.explanation: The excerpt explains that the TLS model relies on a Certificate Authority that is trusted to create proof that a network service is who it claims to be, preventing impostors. For friendly interception, Cilium uses a model similar to traditional firewalls with TLS inspection: the network security team creates their own internal certificate authority to create alternative certificates for external destinations, and each client workload must trust this new certificate. This allows the firewall to act as the destination and inspect traffic.

optionRationale.b: In the standard TLS model, clients do verify certificates; the excerpt states that otherwise the client's TLS library will reject the connection as invalid.
optionRationale.c: In the standard model, a CA signs certificates, not the destination itself; in the Cilium model, the internal CA signs certificates, not the client.
optionRationale.d: The internal CA is not optional for inspection; it is required to create alternative certificates, and it is used for interception, not just logging.

citations.title: A Brief Overview of the TLS Certificate Model
citations.quote: In the case of "friendly interception" for network security monitoring, Cilium uses a model similar to traditional firewalls with TLS inspection capabilities:  the network security team creates their own "internal certificate authority" that can be used to create alternative certificates for external destinations.

questions.stem: An Elasticsearch cluster serves two kinds of client: `outpost` clients that only need to upload troop logs, and an `empire-hq` client that only needs search access to both the `troop_logs` and `spaceship_diagnostics` indices. An engineer wants to apply least privilege security to this cluster. Which statement best describes the goal?

options.text: Give each client access only to the particular indices it needs, and limit the operations each client may perform on each index.
Give every client full access to all indices, but log every request so that misuse can be audited later.
Restrict all clients to search operations only, so that no client can create or modify any index.
Give the `outpost` clients access to both indices and the `empire-hq` client access only to `troop_logs`.

questions.explanation: Least privilege for Elasticsearch clusters means granting each client access only to the particular indices it needs and limiting the operations it may perform on each index. The `outpost` clients need only to upload troop logs, while `empire-hq` needs search access to both indices.

optionRationale.b: Full access for all clients is the opposite of least privilege; auditing does not limit what a compromised client can do.
optionRationale.c: Search-only for everyone would prevent the `outpost` clients from uploading troop logs, which they legitimately need to do.
optionRationale.d: This reverses the stated needs: `outpost` needs only troop-log upload, and `empire-hq` needs search access to both indices.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: For Elasticsearch clusters the **least privilege security** challenge is to give clients access only to particular indices, and to limit the operations each client is allowed to perform on each index.

questions.stem: In an Elasticsearch deployment, the `outpost` clients are intended only to upload troop logs, and the `empire-hq` client is intended only to search both the `troop_logs` and `spaceship_diagnostics` indices. An engineer notes that the outposts are physically exposed and could be captured. What risk does this create for the Elasticsearch data?

options.text: Once an outpost is compromised, its client can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch.
A compromised outpost can only read the `troop_logs` index, because upload credentials never permit search.
A compromised outpost can disrupt Elasticsearch only by exhausting storage with repeated uploads of troop logs.
A compromised outpost has no effect on Elasticsearch, because the `empire-hq` client is the only one with search access.

questions.explanation: The outposts are described as weak spots that are susceptible to capture. Once compromised, the clients can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch, which is exactly what the simulated attack demonstrates.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that a compromised client can search and manipulate critical data; it does not limit the compromise to reading troop logs.
optionRationale.c: Storage exhaustion is not mentioned; the stated risk is searching and manipulating critical data.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly says a compromised outpost client can be used to search and manipulate critical data, so it does affect Elasticsearch.

citations.title: Security Risks for Elasticsearch Access
citations.quote: From the security perspective, the outposts are weak spots and susceptible to be captured by the rebels. Once compromised, the clients can be used to search and manipulate the critical data in Elasticsearch.

questions.stem: Rebels have captured an `outpost` client. Running `kubectl exec outpost -- python search.py`, they retrieve hits from both the `spaceship_diagnostics` index and the `troop_logs` index. They then run `kubectl exec outpost -- python update.py`, which reports uploading spaceship diagnostics with `stats` set to `[OK] [ENGINE OK @SPEED 5000 km/s]`. What has the compromised outpost achieved?

options.text: It has searched all the indices and manipulated the diagnostics data, changing the `stats` for the tiefighter spaceship.
It has only read data, because the `update.py` script failed to modify the diagnostics.
It has modified the `troop_logs` index, leaving the spaceship diagnostics untouched.
It has changed the `spaceshipid` of the tiefighter, so the diagnostics now belong to a different spaceship.

questions.explanation: The excerpt describes the rebels first searching all the indices and then manipulating the diagnostics data from a compromised outpost. The `update.py` run changes the `stats` for the tiefighter spaceship, a change that is hard to detect but has adverse impact.

optionRationale.b: The `update.py` output shows the diagnostics being uploaded with altered `stats`, so the data was modified, not merely read.
optionRationale.c: The manipulation targets `spaceship_diagnostics`, not `troop_logs`.
optionRationale.d: The `spaceshipid` remains `3459B78XNZTF`; what changes is the `stats` field.

The other label pairs belong to the tiefighter and xwing deployments, and k8s-app=kube-dns is the label shown on the DNS endpoints, not on the deathstar pods.

optionRationale.c: org=alliance, class=xwing identifies the alliance ship's client service, not the deathstar pods.

questions.stem: A single-node cluster has Cilium installed and kube-dns working. An engineer deploys the demo application and then runs `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list`. What will the output show?

Only the endpoints running on the same node as the selected Cilium pod, because endpoint listing is always node-local.
Only the deathstar endpoints, because the demo application is the most recently deployed workload.
No endpoints, because endpoint listing requires a multi-node installation.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that in a single-node installation the command `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg endpoint list` lists them all, whereas in a multi-node installation only the endpoints on the same node are listed. Since the scenario is a single-node cluster, every endpoint is shown.

optionRationale.b: Node-local listing is the behaviour described for a multi-node installation, not a single-node one.
optionRationale.c: The command lists endpoints generally; nothing in the excerpt restricts output to the most recently deployed workload.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt describes the command as listing all endpoints in a single-node installation, so it does not require multiple nodes.

questions.stem: An engineer wants to restrict which gRPC methods a set of pods can invoke on a service. How is each gRPC method mapped to an HTTP request so that a Cilium HTTP-aware filter can be applied?

questions.stem: A platform team runs Cilium on a cluster whose nodes are protected by a firewall that blocks all ICMP traffic and all TCP traffic on port 4240 between nodes. No other health-related rules are configured. What is the effect on the cluster?

options.text: Cilium continues to operate, but it cannot provide health information about the nodes.
Cilium fails to start on the nodes until ICMP Type 0/8, Code 0 is permitted.
Cilium continues to operate and health monitoring falls back to UDP port 8472.
Cilium continues to operate but pod-to-pod traffic is blocked until port 4240 is opened.

questions.explanation: Health monitoring via ICMP and TCP 4240 is recommended but optional. If the firewall permits neither method, Cilium still operates, but health information is unavailable.

optionRationale.b: Cilium does not require these rules to start; they are recommended but optional.
optionRationale.c: UDP 8472 is the VXLAN overlay port, not a fallback for health monitoring.
optionRationale.d: Port 4240 is for cilium-health monitoring, not for pod-to-pod traffic forwarding.

questions.stem: A node has 8 vCPUs and 30 GiB of memory. Cilium is started with `--bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio: 0.0025`. What is the resulting size of Cilium's connection tracking BPF maps on that node?

The value 262144 is what kube-proxy would set for its own table on the same node, and 131072 is the minimum floor that applies on smaller nodes.

optionRationale.a: 131072 is the minimum number of entries Cilium uses regardless of memory, which applies to the smaller nodes in the table, not to an 8 vCPU / 30 GiB node.
optionRationale.b: 262144 is the kube-proxy connection tracking entry count for an 8 vCPU / 30 GiB node, not the Cilium count.
optionRationale.d: 569120 is the Cilium connection tracking entry count for a 16 vCPU / 60 GiB node.

options.text: `--bpf-nat-global-max`

questions.stem: An engineer is choosing between the XDP hook and the traffic control ingress hook for a program that must apply L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirect traffic to endpoints. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two hooks?

options.text: The tc ingress hook runs after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet and has access to most of the metadata associated with a packet, making it ideal for local node processing such as L3/L4 endpoint policy.
The tc ingress hook runs before the networking stack has done any processing of the packet, which is why it is preferred for dropping malicious traffic at the driver.
The XDP hook runs after the L3 layer of the stack and therefore has access to more packet metadata than the tc ingress hook.
The XDP hook is attached to a cgroup and runs on TCP events, whereas the tc ingress hook is attached to a networking interface.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that tc ingress programs are attached to a networking interface, same as XDP, but run after the networking stack has done initial processing of the packet, before the L3 layer, with access to most of the packet metadata, which makes the hook ideal for local node processing such as applying L3/L4 endpoint policy and redirecting traffic to endpoints.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the ordering: tc ingress runs after initial processing, not before any processing; running at the driver is the XDP position.
optionRationale.c: XDP is the earliest hook in the driver, not a hook that runs after the L3 layer.
optionRationale.d: The cgroup-attached hook that runs on TCP events is the socket operations hook, not XDP.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
BPF programs attached to the traffic
  control (tc) ingress hook are attached to a networking interface, same as
  XDP, but will run after the networking stack has done initial processing
  of the packet.

questions.stem: Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations program to the root cgroup to monitor TCP state transitions. Which state transition is specifically monitored, and what happens when a socket enters that state?

options.text: The ESTABLISHED transition is monitored, and if the TCP socket has a node local peer a socket send/recv program is attached.
The LISTEN transition is monitored, and a socket send/recv program is detached from the socket.
The ESTABLISHED transition is monitored, and the packet is passed to the Linux xfrm layer for decryption.
The CLOSED transition is monitored, and the socket is redirected to another socket.

questions.explanation: The excerpt says Cilium uses the root-cgroup socket operations program to monitor TCP state transitions, specifically ESTABLISHED, and that when a socket transitions into ESTABLISHED state and has a node local peer (possibly a local proxy) a socket send/recv program is attached.

optionRationale.b: The monitored transition named is ESTABLISHED, and the action described is attaching a program, not detaching one.
optionRationale.c: Passing packets to the Linux xfrm layer belongs to the L3 Encryption object, not the socket operations hook.
optionRationale.d: CLOSED is not the transition named, and redirecting to another socket is a capability of the socket send/recv hook on send operations.

citations.title: Introduction
citations.quote:
Cilium attaches a BPF socket operations
  program to the root cgroup and uses this to monitor for TCP state transitions,
  specifically for ESTABLISHED state transitions.

questions.stem: A platform team enables the eBPF-based ip-masq-agent with ipMasqAgent.enabled=true and supplies a configuration file that sets nonMasqueradeCIDRs but leaves masqLinkLocal unset. Which additional CIDR is appended to the non-masquerade CIDR list?

optionRationale.b: fe80::/10 is the IPv6 link-local range, appended based on masqLinkLocalIPv6 rather than masqLinkLocal.
optionRationale.c: 10.0.0.0/8 is one of the default non-masquerade CIDRs provisioned when the configuration file is empty, not the appended link-local range.
optionRationale.d: 240.0.0.0/4 is likewise one of the default non-masquerade CIDRs, not the appended link-local range.

questions.stem: An engineer runs a Fortio load test against http://echo-service:8080 with the flags `-c 2 -qps 0 -n 20`. The run completes and the summary reports `Code 200 : 19 (95.0 %)` and `Code 503 : 1 (5.0 %)`. What does the presence of the 503 response indicate?

The Fortio pod could not resolve the Service DNS name.
The echo-service pods are all unhealthy and removed from the Service endpoints.
The load test exceeded the 20-call limit and Fortio rejected the extra request.

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that seeing a 503 response code in the output means a circuit breaker has been triggered. The single 503 among 20 calls is therefore the signal that the breaker tripped.

optionRationale.b: Name resolution succeeded: the output shows the address resolved to 10.96.182.43:8080, so DNS failure is not the cause.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the output indicates endpoint removal; the requests reached the Service and returned a mix of 200 and 503.
optionRationale.d: Fortio ran exactly 20 calls as requested; the 503 is a response code from the Service, not a rejection of an over-limit call.

options.text: With perfect keepalive, two sockets would have been used.
With perfect keepalive, three sockets would have been used.
Two sockets were reused and one was closed by the circuit breaker.
The test would have needed two more sockets to avoid the 503 response.

Its ingress rule allows traffic from endpoints with org=empire to port 80 TCP, and its HTTP rules permit only POST /v1/request-landing. A pod labelled class=xwing but without the org=empire label sends a POST request to /v1/request-landing on port 80. What is the expected outcome?

questions.stem: An engineer wants a Cilium L7 policy to allow HTTP requests to any URL under the /v1/ prefix on a service, rather than only the single path /v1/request-landing. How should the path be specified in the policy?

questions.stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy selects pods with app=client and contains an egress rule with toFQDNs.matchPattern set to `*.cilium.io`. The DNS proxy observes a response for `cilium.io` and another for `sub.sub.cilium.io`. Which of these names will have its IPs inserted into the generated L3 rule?

options.text: Neither `cilium.io` nor `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
Both `cilium.io` and `sub.sub.cilium.io`.
`cilium.io` only.
`sub.sub.cilium.io` only.

questions.explanation: The pattern `*.cilium.io` uses a single `*` that matches zero or more valid DNS characters except the `.` separator. It therefore matches `sub.cilium.io` but not `cilium.io` (no leading label) and not `sub.sub.cilium.io` (two labels before the dot). To cover cascaded subdomains the `**.` prefix would be needed.

optionRationale.b: A single `*` does not span the `.` separator, so neither name is covered.
optionRationale.c: `*.cilium.io` requires at least the wildcard label to be present; the bare apex `cilium.io` is explicitly excluded.
optionRationale.d: `sub.sub.cilium.io` has two labels before `cilium.io`, which a single `*` cannot match.

citations.title: DNS based
citations.quote:
``*`` within a domain allows 0 or more valid DNS characters, except for the
    ``.`` separator. ``*.cilium.io`` will match ``sub.cilium.io`` but not
    ``cilium.io`` or ``sub.sub.cilium.io``.
