Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP GET call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /<method-name>/cloudcity.DoorManager.
Each gRPC method is mapped to a raw TCP connection on port 50051 with no HTTP URL.

questions.explanation: Since gRPC is built on top of HTTP, a gRPC call is mapped to an HTTP URL, and each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>. A Cilium HTTP-aware filter can then white-list the permitted URLs.

optionRationale.b: The mapping uses HTTP POST, not GET.
optionRationale.c: The order is /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>, not the reverse.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL, so a URL is involved.

questions.stem: A kind cluster runs in cluster-pool IPAM mode with 10.0.0.0/8 as the cluster-wide pool and /24 per-node PodCIDRs. An engineer performs the Helm upgrade that switches to multi-pool IPAM mode and enables the operator migration, using ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools to create the default CiliumPodIPPool with the same CIDR and mask size. The operator has finished the migration, but no Cilium agent has been restarted yet. What does the engineer observe in each CiliumNode's spec.ipam at this point?

options.text: The podCIDRs field is still populated and pools is empty, because the per-node allocation only moves into pools once the agent restarts.
The podCIDRs field is gone and pools.allocated lists the same per-node CIDR as before, with pool set to default.
Both podCIDRs and pools.allocated are populated, each holding the same per-node CIDR, until the agent restart clears podCIDRs.
pools.allocated is empty and pools.requested lists the number of IPv4 addresses the node needs from the default pool.

The requested block only appears after the agent itself restarts in multi-pool mode.

optionRationale.a: This describes the state before the migration, when each CiliumNode stores its per-node allocation in spec.ipam.podCIDRs and pools is empty; the operator migration has already moved the allocation by the time described.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows the post-migration output with only pools.allocated present, not a period in which both fields carry the same CIDR.

questions.stem: A cluster runs Istio alongside Cilium, which was installed with the Helm values `socketLB.hostNamespaceOnly` and `cni.exclusive=false`. Web servers and clients are deployed across the `red`, `blue` and `green` namespaces, and connectivity checks between all of them return 200. An L4 Cilium network policy is then applied that restricts communication in the `blue` namespace to clients located only in `blue` and `red`. When the same connectivity checks are re-run, which result set should you expect?

options.text: `client 'red' to server 'blue': 200`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 200`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 000` with exit code 28
`client 'red' to server 'blue': 503`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 503`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 000` with exit code 28
`client 'red' to server 'blue': 403`, `client 'blue' to server 'blue': 403`, `client 'green' to server 'blue': 403`
All six checks return 200, because Istio's default `PERMISSIVE` mode overrides the Cilium policy

questions.explanation: The excerpt states that the Cilium-managed L4 policy restricts communication in the `blue` namespace to clients located only in `blue` and `red` namespaces, and the re-run checks show `red` and `blue` clients still reaching `httpbin.blue` with 200 while the `green` client gets 000 and the command terminates with exit code 28. The 503 responses appear only later, once the L7 HTTP policy is added and the Cilium proxy interferes with Istio's mTLS connections.

optionRationale.b: The 503 results belong to the later stage, after the L7 HTTP-based policy is applied and the Cilium proxy interferes with Istio's mTLS-based connections — not to the L4-only policy.
optionRationale.c: 403 is the code seen when a client in `red` requests the `/deny` path after mTLS is disabled and Cilium enforces the L7 policy; it is not the outcome of the L4 restriction on the `blue` namespace.
optionRationale.d: `PERMISSIVE` mode concerns Istio-managed and non-sidecar pods sending and receiving traffic; the excerpt shows the Cilium L4 policy does change the results, with the `green` client failing.

In-use CIDRs can be updated freely, but new CIDRs cannot be added to the pool.
Both adding new CIDRs and deleting in-use CIDRs are permitted, provided the operator is restarted first.
Neither adding new CIDRs nor changing in-use CIDRs is permitted; the pool must be recreated.

This restriction exists to prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes.

questions.stem: A cluster runs Cilium 1.18. Two CiliumBGPAdvertisement objects both select the same LoadBalancer Service, and each sets a different large community. What communities does the resulting BGP advertisement carry?

options.text: Only the communities from the advertisement that appears last in the list of advertisements.
The union of the community elements from every matching advertisement.
Only the communities from the advertisement with the highest local preference.
No communities, because overlapping selectors are rejected and the advertisement is dropped.

questions.explanation: Overlapping advertisement selectors are supported, and for communities the union of elements is taken across all matches. So both large communities end up on the advertisement.

optionRationale.a: Picking the last sequential match describes the behaviour prior to Cilium 1.18, not the current overlap handling.
optionRationale.c: Local preference has its own overlap rule (largest value wins); it does not decide which communities survive.
optionRationale.d: Overlapping selectors are supported today, so the advertisement is not dropped.

questions.stem: A LoadBalancer Service named hello-world initially carries only the label app=hello-world, and two advertisements select on vpc1=true and vpc2=true respectively. What is the BGP advertisement state for this Service at that point?

options.text: It is advertised with the communities of the first advertisement only.
It is advertised with the communities of both advertisements.
It is not advertised at all, because neither selector matches.
It is advertised without any communities attached.

questions.explanation: With no vpc1 or vpc2 label present, neither selector matches, which results in no matches and no BGP advertisements.

optionRationale.a: There is no match to begin with, so no advertisement is produced.
optionRationale.b: Both selectors require labels the Service does not yet have.
optionRationale.d: An unmatched Service is not advertised at all, rather than advertised bare.

attachments.title: The two advertisements
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
 kind: CiliumBGPAdvertisement
 metadata:
   name: bgp-advertisements
   labels:
     advertise: bgp
 spec:
   advertisements:
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: vpc1, operator: In, values: [ "true" ] }
       attributes:
         communities:
           large: [ "1111:1111:1111" ]
     - advertisementType: "Service"
       service:
         addresses:
           - LoadBalancerIP
       selector:
         matchExpressions:
           - { key: vpc2, operator: In, values: [ "true" ] }
       attributes:
         communities:
           large: [ "2222:2222:2222" ]

questions.stem: A platform team wants `cilium monitor` to show DNS query names and HTTP request URLs for traffic leaving pods in the `default` namespace, rather than only packet-level events. Which change achieves this?

options.text: Create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` with L7 rules for the relevant ports, which causes matching flows to be redirected to the proxy.
Restart the Cilium agent with L3/L4 event reporting disabled so that only application-layer events remain.
Add a `matchPattern` entry to the `endpointSelector` of an existing L3/L4 policy.
Run `hubble observe` with the `-t l7` filter, which upgrades captured L3/L4 events into L7 flow details.

questions.explanation: By default the monitor gives visibility only into L3/L4 packet events. To obtain L7 visibility you create a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` that specifies L7 rules; flows matching an L7 rule become visible to Cilium and are redirected to the proxy, so `cilium monitor` or `hubble observe` shows the L7 flow details. Note that such a policy also restricts traffic, so it is not a pure observation tool.

optionRationale.b: Nothing in the excerpt describes disabling L3/L4 reporting; the documented route to L7 visibility is an L7 policy.
optionRationale.c: `matchPattern` belongs under the `dns` rules of a `toPorts` entry, not inside `endpointSelector`, and the selector does not create L7 visibility.
optionRationale.d: The `-t l7` filter selects L7 flows for display; it does not itself produce L7 details, which require the traffic to be proxied by an L7 policy.

questions.stem: An engineer applies the policy below to pods in the `default` namespace. A pod then attempts an HTTP request to an endpoint in the `default` namespace on TCP port 9090. What is the result?

options.text: The request is dropped, because the policy restricts egress and nothing matches the L4 section of either rule.
The request is allowed and appears in `hubble observe` output as an L7 HTTP flow.
The request is allowed but only L3/L4 details are shown, since port 9090 has no L7 rule.
The request is proxied and allowed, because `http: [{}]` matches all ports for endpoints in the `default` namespace.

questions.explanation: The policy restricts egress communication and drops anything that is not matched. The HTTP rule covers only ports TCP/80 and TCP/8080, so traffic to port 9090 matches neither the DNS rule nor the HTTP rule and is dropped.

optionRationale.b: Only traffic on the ports named in the `toPorts` sections is picked up and proxied; port 9090 is not among them.
optionRationale.c: Unmatched egress is dropped rather than allowed, so there is no flow to observe at all.
optionRationale.d: The `http: [{}]` rules apply only to the ports listed in the same `toPorts` entry, namely 80 and 8080.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
   kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
   metadata:
     name: "l7-visibility"
   spec:
     endpointSelector:
       matchLabels:
         "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": default
     egress:
     - toEndpoints:
       - matchLabels:
           "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": kube-system
           "k8s:k8s-app": kube-dns
       toPorts:
       - ports:
         - port: "53"
           protocol: ANY
         rules:
           dns:
           - matchPattern: "*"
     - toEndpoints:
       - matchLabels:
           "k8s:io.kubernetes.pod.namespace": default
       toPorts:
       - ports:
         - port: "80"
           protocol: TCP
         - port: "8080"
           protocol: TCP
         rules:
           http: [{}]

questions.stem: A team is told that adding an L7 `CiliumNetworkPolicy` will let them see HTTP request details in `hubble observe`. What else should they expect from that same policy?

It provides visibility only, leaving the existing L3/L4 allow rules unchanged.
It disables L3/L4 visibility for the selected endpoints so that only L7 events are reported.
It applies only to ingress traffic, since egress visibility is handled by the datapath.

optionRationale.c: L7 policies add proxied L7 flow details; the excerpt does not say L3/L4 visibility is removed.

questions.stem: In the sample output below, what does the `proxy FORWARDED` annotation on the DNS lines indicate about how the traffic was handled?

options.text: The DNS traffic to `kube-dns` on port 53 was redirected to the proxy and forwarded, which is why the L7 query details are visible.
The DNS traffic bypassed the proxy and was forwarded directly by the datapath, with the query details reconstructed afterwards.
The DNS response was dropped by the proxy after the query was forwarded.
The DNS traffic was forwarded by the kernel's connection tracker without involving Cilium.

questions.explanation: The policy causes Cilium to pick up DNS traffic to `kube-dns` on port 53 and redirect it to the proxy, such that the output of `cilium monitor` or `hubble observe` shows the L7 flow details. The `proxy FORWARDED` lines with the DNS Query and DNS Answer are exactly that proxied, forwarded traffic.

optionRationale.b: The `proxy` marker shows the proxy was involved; bypassing it would not yield L7 details.
optionRationale.c: Both the request and the response lines are marked `FORWARDED`, not dropped.
optionRationale.d: The presence of `proxy` in the flow indicates Cilium's proxy handled it, not the connection tracker alone.

questions.stem: A CiliumNetworkPolicy is applied to the pods labelled app=cc-door-mgr. A client pod labelled app=public-terminal calls the gRPC method GetLocation on TCP port 50051, and the call succeeds. Which statement explains why the call was permitted?

options.text: The policy's http rules list a POST to /cloudcity.DoorManager/GetLocation, and requests that match a rule are allowed.
The policy's endpointSelector matches app=public-terminal, so all methods on the client are allowed.
gRPC traffic on port 50051 is always allowed once any CiliumNetworkPolicy selects the port.
The policy denies only methods that are explicitly listed, so unlisted methods such as GetLocation pass by default.

questions.explanation: A CiliumNetworkPolicy contains a list of rules that define allowed requests, so a request is permitted only when it matches one of the listed http rules. GetLocation is one of the three URLs white-listed in the policy, so the call succeeds.

optionRationale.b: The endpointSelector selects the door manager pods (app: cc-door-mgr), not the client; the client is matched by fromEndpoints.
optionRationale.c: Port 50051 is only the port the rule matches; the permitted URLs are white-listed explicitly, so port alone does not allow a call.
optionRationale.d: The logic is inverted: rules define allowed requests, and requests that do not match any rule are denied.

attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: L7 policy to allow public terminals to call GetName, GetLocation, and RequestMaintenance, but not GetState, or SetAccessCode on the Door Manager Service
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cc-door-mgr
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: public-terminal
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "50051"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/GetName"
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/GetLocation"
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/RequestMaintenance"

questions.stem: An engineer wants to restrict a gRPC service so that callers may invoke only a chosen subset of its methods. What must the engineer understand in order to express this as a Cilium HTTP-aware filter?

options.text: How each gRPC call is mapped to an HTTP URL, since each method maps to an HTTP POST to /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.
The numeric gRPC status code that the service returns for each method, since the filter matches on status codes.
The TLS certificate subject used by the gRPC server, since the filter matches on the server identity.
The protobuf message schema of each request, since the filter matches on serialised message fields.

questions.explanation: Because gRPC is built on top of HTTP, a subset of methods can be allowed by understanding how a gRPC call is mapped to an HTTP URL and then applying a Cilium HTTP-aware filter. Each gRPC method is mapped to an HTTP POST call to a URL of the form /cloudcity.DoorManager/<method-name>.

optionRationale.b: Status codes appear in the client output after a denial; the filter itself matches method and path, not status codes.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes matching on HTTP method and URL path, not on any certificate identity.
optionRationale.d: The filter operates on the HTTP URL mapping, not on protobuf message contents.

Since gRPC build on top of HTTP, this can be achieved easily by understanding how a
gRPC call is mapped to an HTTP URL, and then applying a Cilium HTTP-aware filter to
allow public terminals to only invoke a subset of all the total gRPC methods available
on the door service.

questions.stem: A public terminal calls the gRPC method GetStatus on the door service. The policy shown is in force. What is the outcome, and why?

options.text: The request is denied, because it does not match any of the listed http rules and requests that do not match any rule are denied as invalid.
The request is allowed, because GetStatus is not named in the policy and therefore is not restricted.
The request is allowed, because the policy only restricts the SetAccessCode method.
The request is denied, because the policy's description explicitly lists GetStatus as forbidden.

questions.explanation: The policy's http rules white-list only GetName, GetLocation and RequestMaintenance. A CiliumNetworkPolicy contains a list of rules that define allowed requests, so a request that matches none of them, such as GetStatus, is denied as invalid.

optionRationale.b: Unlisted requests are not implicitly allowed; the rules define what is allowed, and everything else is denied.
optionRationale.c: The policy does not single out SetAccessCode; it white-lists three URLs and denies everything else, including GetStatus.
optionRationale.d: The description mentions GetState and SetAccessCode, not GetStatus, and a description does not enforce anything.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: L7 policy to allow public terminals to call GetName, GetLocation, and RequestMaintenance, but not GetState, or SetAccessCode on the Door Manager Service
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: cc-door-mgr
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        app: public-terminal
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "50051"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/GetName"
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/GetLocation"
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/cloudcity.DoorManager/RequestMaintenance"

questions.stem: A cluster administrator applies the following CiliumBGPClusterConfig. Which nodes will the BGP Control Plane configure with the instance named instance-65000?

options.text: Only nodes whose labels match rack: rack0
Every node in the cluster, because no nodeSelector is honoured for BGP instances
Only the node running the Cilium agent that first reconciles the resource
Only nodes that also carry the label cilium.io/bgp: enabled

questions.explanation: The CiliumBGPClusterConfig defines BGP configuration for one or more nodes in the cluster based on its nodeSelector field. In the manifest the nodeSelector uses matchLabels with rack: rack0, so only nodes carrying that label are configured with the instance.

optionRationale.b: The nodeSelector field is precisely what scopes the configuration to a subset of nodes; it is not ignored.
optionRationale.c: The resource is not bound to a single reconciling node; it selects nodes by label.
optionRationale.d: No such label is mentioned; the selector in the manifest is rack: rack0.

questions.stem: A team runs Cilium 1.16 in a development cluster where no LoadBalancer Service implementation is available. They enable the Cilium ingress controller's host network mode through Helm. Which statement describes the resulting behaviour?

options.text: The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is disabled automatically, and the Envoy listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6).
The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode remains active alongside host network mode, and the Envoy listener is exposed only on the node's primary interface.
The LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode is disabled automatically, and the Envoy listener is exposed only on the loopback interface (127.0.0.1 for IPv4 and/or ::1 for IPv6).
Host network mode cannot be enabled unless a LoadBalancer Service is available, so the Helm installation fails.

questions.explanation: Enabling host network mode automatically disables the LoadBalancer/NodePort type Service mode, because the two are mutually exclusive, and the listener is then exposed on all interfaces — 0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6. This suits environments where a LoadBalancer Service is unavailable, such as development clusters.

optionRationale.b: The two modes are mutually exclusive, so LoadBalancer/NodePort Service mode is disabled rather than kept active, and the listener binds all interfaces rather than a single primary one.
optionRationale.c: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 and/or ::), not restricted to the loopback interface.
optionRationale.d: Host network mode is specifically useful where a LoadBalancer Service is unavailable, so it does not require one to exist.

questions.stem: A cluster-wide policy named default-deny is applied. It selects every endpoint whose io.kubernetes.pod.namespace is not kube-system, and its only egress rule permits UDP port 53 to the kube-dns endpoints in kube-system with a DNS matchPattern of '*'. A client outside the cluster then requests the /details endpoint of an application exposed through Cilium Ingress. What is the result?

options.text: The request is denied, and the response returned to the client is HTTP 403.
The request is allowed, because the policy contains no ingress section and therefore only restricts egress.
The request is allowed, because the reserved:ingress identity is excluded from the endpointSelector.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so the client receives no HTTP response at all.

questions.explanation: The policy denies all traffic by default, and the excerpt states that with it applied the request to /details is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The captured session shows the client receiving an HTTP 403 Forbidden with server: envoy, so the denial is surfaced as an HTTP response rather than a silent connection failure.

optionRationale.b: The policy is described as blocking all traffic by default; the absence of an ingress section does not leave ingress unrestricted, and the observed result is a denial.
optionRationale.c: The endpointSelector excludes only the kube-system namespace; nothing in the policy exempts the reserved:ingress identity, which is handled by a separate policy later in the flow.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows a complete HTTP exchange ending in 403 Forbidden, not a dropped connection.

attachments.title: The default-deny policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "default-deny"
spec:
  description: "Block all the traffic (except DNS) by default"
  egress:
  - toEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: kube-system
        k8s-app: kube-dns
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: '53'
        protocol: UDP
      rules:
        dns:
        - matchPattern: '*'
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: io.kubernetes.pod.namespace
      operator: NotIn
      values:
      - kube-system

questions.stem: After a default-deny policy has blocked traffic to an application behind Cilium Ingress, a second CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy named allow-ingress-egress is applied. It selects endpoints for which reserved:ingress exists and allows egress to the cluster entity. What effect does this have?

options.text: It allows the ingress proxy to reach endpoints in the cluster, so requests to /details succeed from both an external client and an in-cluster client.
It allows only external traffic, because the cluster entity covers endpoints outside the cluster rather than inside it.
It has no effect until the default-deny policy is deleted, because cluster-wide policies are evaluated in creation order.
It allows the ingress proxy to reach the cluster, but in-cluster clients remain blocked because they do not carry the reserved:ingress identity.

questions.explanation: The policy grants egress from the reserved:ingress identity to all cluster identities, and the captured session shows both the external curl and the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the /details payload. The excerpt notes that allowing all traffic from reserved:ingress to all cluster identities is generally the more reliable option, since Cilium Ingress is part of the networking infrastructure.

optionRationale.b: The policy targets the cluster entity, and the excerpt's own output shows the in-cluster client succeeding, so the rule is not limited to external traffic.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the excerpt describes creation-order evaluation or a requirement to delete the default-deny policy first; the allow policy takes effect alongside it.
optionRationale.d: The captured output shows the in-cluster client from deployment/client receiving the same JSON payload, so in-cluster traffic is no longer blocked.

attachments.title: The allow policy
attachments.body:
---
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-egress
spec:
  description: "Allow all the egress traffic from reserved ingress identity to any endpoints in the cluster"
  endpointSelector:
    matchExpressions:
    - key: reserved:ingress
      operator: Exists
  egress:
  - toEntities:
    - cluster

questions.stem: A cluster runs the CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy shown in the attachment. A pod with labels org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace is scheduled on node1 and sends traffic to an external address. What happens to that traffic?

options.text: It is routed through node2 and SNATed with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.
It is SNATed on node1 using the first IPv4 address of the interface enp0s8.
It leaves the cluster without SNAT because the destination 0.0.0.0/0 is not matched by the policy.
It is dropped because the pod is not on the gateway node.

questions.explanation: The policy selects pods with org=empire and class=mediabot in the default namespace, and its nodeSelector restricts it to node1. Traffic from those pods on node1 to 0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0 is routed through the gateway node labelled node.kubernetes.io/name: node2, which SNATs it with the egress IP 10.168.60.100.

optionRationale.b: The interface field is only an alternative to egressIP; here egressIP is set, so the interface is not used.
optionRationale.c: The policy explicitly lists 0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0 as destinationCIDRs, so all traffic leaving the cluster is matched.
optionRationale.d: The policy routes traffic through the gateway node; it does not drop traffic from pods on other nodes.

attachments.title: The egress gateway policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: cilium.io/v2
kind: CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy
metadata:
  name: egress-sample
spec:
  # Specify which pods should be subject to the current policy.
  # Multiple pod selectors can be specified.
  selectors:
  - podSelector:
      matchLabels:
        org: empire
        class: mediabot
        # The following label selects default namespace
        io.kubernetes.pod.namespace: default
    nodeSelector: # optional, if not specified the policy applies to all nodes
      matchLabels:
        node.kubernetes.io/name: node1 # only traffic from this node will be SNATed
  # Specify which destination CIDR(s) this policy applies to.
  # Multiple CIDRs can be specified.
  destinationCIDRs:
  - "0.0.0.0/0"
  - "::/0"

  # Configure the gateway node.
  egressGateway:
    # Specify which node should act as gateway for this policy.

options.text: 120 seconds
15 seconds
Until the Cilium Agent sends a new BGP OPEN message, with no timer involved
The routes are withdrawn immediately, because no RestartTime was configured

questions.explanation: The excerpt gives the default explicitly: the default value of RestartTime is 120 seconds. The timer starts when the peer receives the TCP FIN and moves to Idle, and the routes are removed when it expires.

optionRationale.b: 15 seconds appears only in the example manifest as an explicitly configured restartTimeSeconds value, not as a default.
optionRationale.c: The peer starts its RestartTime timer on receiving the TCP FIN; the wait is bounded by that timer rather than by the next OPEN message.
optionRationale.d: Graceful restart is what prevents immediate withdrawal; the default timer still applies when restartTimeSeconds is omitted.

questions.stem: A Cilium Agent managing BGP peering is restarted. The peering router receives a TCP FIN on the BGP session. What does the router do, and what happens to traffic in the datapath while the Agent restarts?

questions.stem: A cluster's Cilium Agent takes roughly 40 seconds to boot after a restart. You want the peering BGP router to keep the routes it learned from the Cilium BGP control plane for as long as possible during that restart, but you also want the peer to remove them if the Agent fails to come back. Which configuration should you apply?

options.text: A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 15`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: false` and `restartTimeSeconds: 60`
A CiliumBGPPeerConfig with `gracefulRestart.enabled: true` and no `restartTimeSeconds`, relying on the 120-second default

questions.explanation: `RestartTime` is the time advertised to the peer within which the Cilium BGP control plane is expected to re-establish the BGP session after a restart, and on its expiration the peer removes the routes previously advertised. Because the Agent here needs about 40 seconds to boot, the value must be greater than that boot time, so 60 seconds is the suitable choice. A value of 15 seconds would expire before the Agent is back, and the default of 120 seconds is not the tightest fit for the stated requirement.

optionRationale.a: 15 seconds is shorter than the roughly 40-second boot time, so the peer's timer would expire and the routes would be removed before the session is re-established.
optionRationale.c: Graceful restart must be enabled for the capability to be advertised and for the peer to hold routes; disabling it defeats the purpose.
optionRationale.d: The 120-second default is valid, but the question asks for the setting that keeps routes only as long as needed while still covering the boot time, which 60 seconds does more precisely.

questions.stem: A cluster runs in Multi-Pool IPAM mode. A pod is created in a namespace that carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=green-pool, while the pod itself carries the annotation ipam.cilium.io/ip-pool=blue-pool. Both pools exist and both have selectors that would match the pod. Which pool is the pod's IP allocated from?

options.text: blue-pool, because the annotation on the pod takes precedence over the annotation on the namespace
green-pool, because the namespace annotation is evaluated first
The default pool, because conflicting annotations are ignored
Allocation fails, because the pod matches more than one pool

questions.explanation: The explicit pool annotation is the first item in the precedence order, and it may be placed either on the pod or on the namespace of the pod. The pod's own annotation is the one that names the pool, so blue-pool is used; the namespace annotation does not override it.

optionRationale.b: The namespace annotation is an alternative place to put the explicit pool name, not a higher-priority source than the pod's own annotation.
optionRationale.c: The default pool is only used when neither the pod nor the namespace has an explicit pool annotation, or when no selectors match.
optionRationale.d: The exactly-one-pool rule applies to matching pools via selectors; here the pool is named explicitly by annotation.

optionRationale.c: allowFirstIP controls whether the first address of an allocated CIDR is allocatable; it has nothing to do with pool selection.

Because the headless service is required to give the Cilium agent pods a stable cluster IP for scraping.

questions.stem: An engineer configures Prometheus with a `kubernetes-pods` job using the `pod` role and the relabel rules shown, expecting Cilium and Envoy metrics to be picked up automatically. Which relabel configuration makes that automatic discovery work?

options.text: A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule combining `__address__` and `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into `__address__`.
A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule writing the port into `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape`.

A `drop` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule combining `__address__` and `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into `__address__`.
A `keep` rule on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, plus a `replace` rule writing `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` into the `job` label.

questions.explanation: The excerpt shows the `scrape_configs` snippet in which a `keep` action filters on `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape` with regex `true`, and a `replace` action uses `__address__` together with `__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port` to set `__address__`. With that configuration Prometheus picks up the Cilium and Envoy metrics automatically.

optionRationale.b: The keep rule is applied to the scrape annotation, not the port annotation, and the replace rule targets `__address__`.
optionRationale.c: A `drop` action would discard the very pods carrying the scrape annotation.
optionRationale.d: The replace rule sets `__address__`, not the `job` label.

scrape_configs:

   kubernetes_sd_configs:
   - role: pod
   relabel_configs:
     - source_labels: [__meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_scrape]
       action: keep
       regex: true
     - source_labels: [__address__, __meta_kubernetes_pod_annotation_prometheus_io_port]
       action: replace
       regex: ([^:]+)(?::\d+)?;(\d+)
       replacement: ${1}:${2}
       target_label: __address__

questions.stem: An administrator applies the following policy. Which statement describes its effect?

options.text: Ingress from the world entity is denied on all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces, while traffic from everywhere else, including existing inter-cluster policies, is still allowed.
All ingress to every pod is denied, because the endpointSelector is empty and therefore matches everything.
Ingress from the world entity is denied only in the namespace where the policy is created, because it is a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy.
Ingress from the world entity is denied, and all other ingress is also denied because no allow rule is present.

questions.explanation: The policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy with an empty endpointSelector, so it applies to all pods managed by Cilium in all namespaces. Its ingressDeny blocks the world entity, while the ingress rule allows the all entity, so traffic from everywhere except world continues to be permitted and existing inter-cluster policies are still allowed.

optionRationale.b: The empty endpointSelector widens the set of selected pods, but the policy denies only the world entity rather than all ingress.
optionRationale.c: The resource is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy, not a namespaced CiliumNetworkPolicy, so its effect is cluster-wide.
optionRationale.d: The policy includes an ingress rule allowing the all entity, so other ingress is not denied.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "external-lockdown"
spec:
  endpointSelector: {}
  ingressDeny:
  - fromEntities:
    - "world"
  ingress:
  - fromEntities:
    - "all"

questions.stem: A team wants to write a deny policy that blocks requests to a specific URL path on an otherwise allowed service, and another that blocks traffic to a specific external domain name. What does Cilium support here?

options.text: Neither is supported: deny policies cannot enforce at Layer 7, so a URL cannot be specifically denied, and toFQDNs cannot be used to deny traffic to a specific domain name.
Both are supported, provided the deny policy is a CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy rather than a namespaced one.
Denying a URL is supported at Layer 7, but denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is not.
Denying a specific domain name with toFQDNs is supported, but denying a URL at Layer 7 is not.

questions.explanation: Deny policies do not support policy enforcement at Layer 7, which means specifically denying a URL is not possible, and they do not support toFQDNs, which means specifically denying traffic to a specific domain name is not possible either.

optionRationale.b: The limitation applies to deny policies generally; using a clusterwide policy does not add Layer 7 or toFQDNs deny support.
optionRationale.c: Layer 7 enforcement, including denying a URL, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.
optionRationale.d: toFQDNs, that is denying traffic to a specific domain name, is explicitly not supported by deny policies.

questions.stem: An engineer sets `connectRetryTimeSeconds: 5` on a BGP peer configuration to speed up reconnection after losing connectivity. What range of values can the actual ConnectRetryTimer take?

options.text: Exactly 5 seconds, because the configured value is used as-is
Anywhere from 5 up to but not including 10 seconds, because random jitter is applied internally
Anywhere from 0 up to but not including 5 seconds, because jitter is subtracted from the configured value
Exactly 10 seconds, because the configured value is always doubled

questions.explanation: Random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, so the actual value used for the ConnectRetryTimer falls within the interval `[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)`. With a configured value of 5, that is from 5 up to but not including 10.

optionRationale.a: Jitter is applied internally, so the configured value is not used verbatim.
optionRationale.c: The interval starts at the configured value, not below it; jitter is not subtracted.
optionRationale.d: The upper bound of the interval is exclusive, and the value is not fixed at double the configured value.

citations.title: Timers
citations.quote:
As random jitter is applied to the configured value internally, the actual value used for the
``ConnectRetryTimer`` is within the interval ``[ConnectRetryTimeSeconds, 2 * ConnectRetryTimeSeconds)``.

questions.stem: A BGP peer configuration is created without specifying any timer values. What KeepaliveTimer does the BGP Control Plane use?

options.text: 3 seconds
9 seconds
30 seconds
120 seconds

questions.explanation: The default for the KeepaliveTimer, set by `keepAliveTimeSeconds`, is 30. The values 3 and 9 are the minimum possible values recommended for datacenter deployments, and 120 is the default for the ConnectRetryTimer.

optionRationale.a: 3 is the minimum possible value recommended for datacenter networks, not the default.
optionRationale.b: 9 is the minimum possible value recommended for the hold timer, not the keepalive default.
optionRationale.d: 120 is the default for the ConnectRetryTimer, not the KeepaliveTimer.

questions.stem: A node has a loopback interface named lo carrying the address 10.0.0.5/32, and the interface is administratively enabled and operationally up. A CiliumBGPAdvertisement with advertisementType "Interface" and interface name lo is applied. What does the BGP control plane advertise to peers for this interface?

options.text: The exact route 10.0.0.5/32.
The connected subnet route 10.0.0.0/24.
Nothing, because addresses on the loopback range are never advertised.
Nothing, because Cilium does not manage addresses on non-Cilium-owned interfaces.

questions.explanation: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes, so a /32 address on the interface becomes a /32 prefix. The exclusion list covers addresses from the loopback, multicast, IPv6 link-local and IPv4-mapped IPv6 address ranges — 10.0.0.5 is not in any of those ranges, so it is advertised. The fact that Cilium does not manage addresses on arbitrary interfaces only means the administrator must configure them; it does not prevent advertisement.

optionRationale.b: Interface IPs are advertised as exact routes (/32 or /128 prefixes), not as the covering subnet prefix.
optionRationale.c: The loopback range is excluded, but 10.0.0.5 is a regular address, not a loopback-range address; the interface merely happens to be named lo.
optionRationale.d: Cilium not managing the addresses means the node administrator configures them; it does not stop the BGP control plane advertising them.

A policy whose `targetRefs` entry has `kind: Service`, `name: backend` and `sectionName: https`, and whose `validation` sets `hostname: backend` with `caCertificateRefs` pointing at the `example-ca` ConfigMap.

A pod labelled org=empire, class=deathstar runs the deathstar service, and a pod labelled org=empire runs tiefighter. An engineer then runs `kubectl exec tiefighter -- curl -s -XPUT deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port`. What does the command return?

options.text: Access denied
Panic: deathstar exploded, followed by a goroutine trace
Ship landed
Nothing at all; the connection times out

questions.explanation: The policy restricts tiefighter to a single HTTP call, POST /v1/request-landing, and disallows all other calls, including PUT /v1/exhaust-port. Re-running the exhaust-port test therefore yields "Access denied" rather than the panic that occurred before the L7 rule existed.

optionRationale.b: That is the outcome of the same PUT request before the L7-aware policy is applied, when tiefighter had full access to deathstar's API.
optionRationale.c: That is the response to the permitted POST /v1/request-landing call, not to the disallowed PUT /v1/exhaust-port.
optionRationale.d: A timeout is what happens to traffic from pods without the label org=empire, such as xwing; tiefighter carries that label, so its request is evaluated by the HTTP rule and denied.

    toPorts:

        - method: "POST"

questions.stem: A kind cluster is being migrated from cluster-pool IPAM to multi-pool IPAM. The operator has already created the default CiliumPodIPPool and performed the migration, and the Cilium agent on kind-worker has been restarted. You then run `kubectl get ciliumnode kind-worker -o yaml | yq .spec.ipam` and see the output in the attachment. What does the `requested` section tell you?

options.text: The restarted agent is running in multi-pool IPAM mode and is requesting 16 IPv4 addresses from the default pool, while the previously allocated 10.0.3.0/24 CIDR is preserved.
The agent is still running in cluster-pool mode and is asking the operator to reserve 16 additional per-node PodCIDRs from the default pool.
The operator has failed to migrate the node and is requesting 16 replacement addresses because the 10.0.3.0/24 allocation is about to be released.
The node is requesting 16 new pools to be created, each with a /24 mask size, before the agent can start allocating pod IPs.

questions.explanation: After the agent restarts it runs in multi-pool IPAM mode and requests IPs from the default pool while preserving the IPs of restored endpoints. The output shows the same per-node CIDR (10.0.3.0/24) still allocated from the default pool, with a new `requested` entry asking for 16 IPv4 addresses from that pool.

optionRationale.b: The `requested` block appears only after the agent restarts into multi-pool mode; it is not a cluster-pool request for extra PodCIDRs, and the `allocated` entry already shows the node's CIDR.
optionRationale.c: Nothing in the output indicates a failed migration or a pending release of 10.0.3.0/24; that CIDR remains allocated from the default pool.
optionRationale.d: `needed: ipv4-addrs: 16` is a request for addresses from the existing default pool, not a request to create 16 new pools.

attachments.title: IPAM state of kind-worker after the agent restart
attachments.body:
$ kubectl get ciliumnode kind-worker -o yaml | yq .spec.ipam
  pools:
    allocated:
      - cidrs:
          - 10.0.3.0/24
        pool: default
    requested:
      - needed:
          ipv4-addrs: 16
        pool: default

questions.stem: A platform team has enabled Cilium's bandwidth manager on a cluster and wants to confirm, from the command line, that the feature is active and see which devices are enforcing egress limits. Which command and output line should they look for?

options.text: Run `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager` and look for a line such as `BandwidthManager:       EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]`.
Run `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager` and look for a line such as `BandwidthManager:       TBF [eth0]`.
Run `kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l k8s-app=cilium` and confirm that every Cilium Pod reports `1/1 Running`.
Run `kubectl -n kube-system exec ds/cilium -- cilium-dbg status | grep BandwidthManager` and look for a line such as `BandwidthManager:       EDT with BPF [CUBIC] [eth0]`.

questions.explanation: The `cilium status` CLI command exposes the feature through the `BandwidthManager` info line, and it also dumps the list of devices on which egress bandwidth limitation is enforced. The documented example output is `BandwidthManager:       EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]`, so the team should look for that form.

optionRationale.b: TBF (Token Bucket Filter) is the basis of the bandwidth CNI plugin, which Cilium's bandwidth manager does not use; the status line reports EDT with BPF, not TBF.
optionRationale.c: Checking that the Cilium Pods are running only verifies that the agents came up; it does not show whether the bandwidth manager feature is enabled or which devices enforce egress limits.
optionRationale.d: The status line reports the congestion control in brackets, and the documented example shows BBR, not CUBIC.

They want to confirm that the feature is active and see which devices are enforcing the egress limit. Which command and output line should they look for?

In the documented example the line reads `BandwidthManager:       EDT with BPF [BBR] [eth0]`, showing EDT with BPF, the BBR congestion control and the device `eth0`.

optionRationale.b: The bandwidth manager uses EDT rather than the TBF (Token Bucket Filter) approach associated with the bandwidth CNI plugin, so the status line would not report TBF.

optionRationale.d: The documented status line includes the congestion control in brackets alongside the device, so a line showing only the device does not match the expected output.

questions.stem: The CiliumNetworkPolicy rule1 shown in the attachment is applied in the default namespace. A pod labelled org=empire, class=deathstar runs the deathstar service. An empire ship pod labelled org=empire sends a PUT request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/exhaust-port, and a pod labelled org=rebel sends a POST request to deathstar.default.svc.cluster.local/v1/request-landing. What happens in each case?

options.text: The PUT from the empire ship is answered with "Access denied", while the request from the pod without the org=empire label is dropped and the connection times out.
The PUT from the empire ship is answered with "Access denied", and the request from the pod without the org=empire label is also answered with "Access denied".
The PUT from the empire ship reaches the maintenance API and the deathstar panics, because the policy only restricts POST requests.
The PUT from the empire ship is dropped and the connection times out, while the request from the pod without the org=empire label is answered with "Access denied".

questions.explanation: The policy restricts tiefighter to a single allowed HTTP call, POST /v1/request-landing, and disallows all other calls, so the PUT to /v1/exhaust-port is rejected at L7 with "Access denied". Because the rule also builds on the identity-aware rule, traffic from pods that do not carry the org=empire label is still dropped at the identity level, so the connection simply times out rather than returning an HTTP error.

optionRationale.b: The L7 denial message applies only to traffic that is already permitted by identity; pods outside org=empire never reach the HTTP proxy, so they time out instead of receiving "Access denied".
optionRationale.c: The whole point of the L7 policy is to disallow all calls other than POST /v1/request-landing, explicitly including PUT /v1/exhaust-port, so the panic is prevented rather than permitted.
optionRationale.d: The two outcomes are swapped: the labelled empire ship is the one subject to the HTTP rule and gets "Access denied", while the unlabelled pod is dropped by identity and times out.

attachments.title: The policy under test
attachments.body:
apiVersion: "cilium.io/v2"
kind: CiliumNetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: "rule1"
spec:
  description: "L7 policy to restrict access to specific HTTP call"
  endpointSelector:
    matchLabels:
      org: empire
      class: deathstar
  ingress:
  - fromEndpoints:
    - matchLabels:
        org: empire
    toPorts:
    - ports:
      - port: "80"
        protocol: TCP
      rules:
        http:
        - method: "POST"
          path: "/v1/request-landing"

questions.stem: A kind cluster is being migrated from cluster-pool IPAM to multi-pool IPAM. The Helm upgrade has already been run with `ipam.mode=multi-pool`, `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.default.ipv4.cidrs='{10.0.0.0/8}'`, `ipam.operator.autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools.default.ipv4.maskSize=24` and `extraConfig.enable-cluster-pool-to-multi-pool-migration=true`, and the operator has been restarted. The Cilium agents have not yet been restarted. An engineer inspects `kind-worker` and sees the output in the attachment. What does this output indicate about the state of that node?

options.text: The operator has performed the migration: the node's per-node CIDR is now allocated from the `default` multi-pool IP pool, but the agent is still running in cluster-pool mode until it is restarted.
The migration has not started on this node, because `spec.ipam.pools` is populated only after the Cilium agent itself is restarted in multi-pool mode.
The node has already been fully migrated and its agent restarted, because a `requested` entry for the `default` pool appears alongside the allocation.
The node has lost its per-node PodCIDR, because the `podCIDRs` field is no longer present and no replacement allocation has been made.

questions.explanation: The output shows `spec.ipam.pools.allocated` with the CIDR `10.0.3.0/24` and `pool: default`, which is the post-migration shape: after the operator performs the migration, each node has the same per-node CIDR allocated from the default multi-pool IP pool. There is no `requested` section, which only appears once the agent has restarted and is requesting IPs from the default pool. The excerpt notes that cluster-pool agents continue to use their existing cluster-pool allocations until they are restarted, so the node is migrated at the operator level while its agent still runs in cluster-pool mode.

optionRationale.b: The `pools` field is already populated in the output, and the excerpt shows it being filled by the operator's migration before any agent restart is described.
optionRationale.c: A `requested` entry appears only after the agent restarts, as shown in the later output where the agent requests `ipv4-addrs: 16` from the `default` pool; the attached output has no such entry.
optionRationale.d: The CIDR is not lost: it has moved from `spec.ipam.podCIDRs` into `spec.ipam.pools.allocated` with `pool: default`, preserving the same `10.0.3.0/24` value.
